courses.description: This course traces the history of art and architecture in premodern East Asia, emphasizing ideas and ways of seeing and representing that were common or different across East Asia.

courses.title: The Film Experience: Introduction to the Visual Study of Film
courses.description: A critical and historical introduction to film from a visual arts perspective. The course surveys the history of film from its inception to the present, drawing upon both foreign and American traditions.

courses.title: Introduction to the Art and Architecture of Pre-Hispanic Mesoamerica
courses.description: This course introduces the art, architecture, and cultures of Pre-Hispanic Mesoamerica, from the rise of Mesoamerica's first high civilization in the second millennium BCE to the defeat of the Aztec Empire in 1521 CE. Honors version available.

courses.title: Introduction to American Art
courses.description: This course surveys American art, architecture, and material culture from early European exploration of the Americas to the 1960s. Previously offered as ARTH 261.

courses.title: Pencils to Pixels: The History of Animation
courses.description: This course examines the history and development of animation as an art form and an industry worldwide. It covers early experiments with animation, the transition to sound and feature films, and the rise of classical Hollywood studios. Course material will extend to other countries or regions. Work created outside the industry, such as experimental, cult, fine art, and video game animation, will also be considered. The course will track the development of the technology and techniques of animation, such as cel animation, stop-motion animation, puppet animation, silhouette animation, rotoscoping, pixilation, direct animation, limited animation on TV, and computer animation.

courses.title: Special Topics in Art History, FC-AESTH
courses.description: Selected topics in art history.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: Art and Fashion from Rome to Timbuktu
courses.description: In the Roman Empire and in contemporary Africa, clothing reflects local symbolic systems and global trade networks. Rome is imagined as the source of Western culture, and Africa evokes distant exoticism; this course will complicate such conceptions. Through fashion we explore political, economic, and religious systems, as well as creativity.

courses.title: Making Material Histories: A Makerspace Course
courses.description: This course explores the history and technology of materials from wood and glass to steel and plastic in art, culture, and science. Students will engage with materials both through hands-on fabrication at BeAM and through researching historical debates surrounding material invention and use by artists, scientists, and industries.

courses.title: The Visual Culture of News, Past and Present
courses.description: Focusing on Western news production from early modernity to the present, this class considers the news as a visual object, examining the different formats and media of news, the design of the page/pamphlet/screen, the way images are incorporated, and the relationship of all of this to written text.

courses.title: Art and Archaeology of the Ancient Near East
courses.description: A survey of the cultures of the ancient Near East, Mesopotamia, Anatolia (modern Turkey), and the Levant, from the first settled villages of the ninth millennium to the Persian conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE.

courses.title: Empires of the Nile: The Archaeology of Egypt and Nubia
courses.description: A survey of the archaeological remains of ancient Egypt and Nubia, from late prehistory through the first millennium BCE.

courses.title: Greek Art and Archaeology
courses.description: The historical development of the art and architecture of Greece from the Bronze Age through the Hellenistic period.

courses.title: Roman Art and Archaeology
courses.description: This course explores the archaeology of the Roman world between the eighth century BCE and the fifth century CE, focusing on issues of urbanization, trade and consumption, colonization, and the Roman army.

courses.title: Objects, Museums, and Meanings
courses.description: This course explores objects and meaning in the context of museums. How does one "read" an object? What do works of art communicate on their own, and how do a series of decisions - made by individuals and institutions - shape how we understand them? Through museum visits, object-based learning and research, readings, and discussion, this course will consider how objects, and their collection and display, shape our understanding of the world around us. Honors version available.

courses.title: Art History in Motion: Looking, Hearing, Sensing
courses.description: This class investigates bringing awareness to the way we move and our sensorial experiences as vital complements to other methodological approaches to art historical interpretation. It does so through an examination of a variety of artworks in their historical contexts, different movement explorations, and analysis of interpretative methods. Attending both to art and ourselves in this way, we can question, challenge, and expand the ways in which we know the world. Honors version available.

courses.title: Women in the Visual Arts I
courses.description: This course analyzes the role of women in Western art as art producers and consumers of art and looks at how women have been represented.

courses.title: African Art and Culture
courses.description: African art is deeply embedded in African societies, past and present. Artistic practices are integral to politics, religion, social status, economics, and self-expression. The course explores masquerades, sculpture, architecture, dress, rural and urban arts, and contemporary practices to understand how art functions as a dynamic social and cultural force. We will view artworks at the Ackland Art Museum, and we will invite artists and scholars to visit our class in person and/or via zoom.

courses.title: Chinese Art and Culture: From Song to Qing
courses.description: Organized around eight key themes, the course highlights the multifaceted character and vibrant textures of Chinese art from the Song dynasty (960-1279) to the Qing dynasty (1644-1912). Students will study canonized genres--landscape representation, court and literati practices--while also engaging with topics often marginalized in survey narratives, including depictions of animals and the varied roles women assumed within artistic worlds.

courses.title: Medieval Art in Western Europe
courses.description: Survey of major developments in painting and sculpture in Europe during the Latin Middle Ages (300-1400 CE).

courses.title: Medieval Iconography
courses.description: Required preparation, any introductory art history course or permission of the instructor. Understanding the meaning of medieval art by examining the iconography of selected important works. Honors version available.

courses.title: From Alexander to Cleopatra: Hellenistic Art and Archaeology
courses.description: Survey of the archaeology of the Hellenistic Mediterranean from the time of Alexander the Great until the Roman conquest (350-31 BCE), with emphasis on art and architecture of cities and sanctuaries.

courses.title: Cathedrals, Abbeys, Castles: Gothic Art and Architecture (c. 1130-1450)
courses.description: This course covers the development of Gothic church and secular architecture in Europe between 1130 and 1500. It explores the formal and constructive progress in architecture (including its decoration: sculpture, stained glass windows) as well as the social, political, and economic aspects of medieval society that affected these developments.

courses.title: Northern European Art: Van Eyck to Bruegel
courses.description: Required preparation, any introductory art history course or permission of the instructor. Survey of painting and sculpture ca. 1400-1600 in the Netherlands--Belgium (Flanders) and Holland--as well as France and England.

courses.title: European Baroque Art
courses.description: Required preparation, any introductory art history course or permission of the instructor. This course examines 17th-century art and architecture in Europe.

courses.title: 18th-Century Art
courses.description: An introductory survey of 18th century European visual culture, from painting and sculpture to art markets and the decorative arts. This class works closely with art objects in person at the Ackland Museum of Art and Wilson Special Collections. Central themes in the class include Europe's relationship to the world, the sociology of the art world, and how art objects are made.

courses.title: Art and Architecture of Viceregal Latin America
courses.description: This course surveys the art and architecture of Hispanophone and Lusophone America of the Viceregal period (1492-ca. 1810).

courses.title: The Arts in England, 1450-1650
courses.description: This course explores the visual culture of England during the reigns of the Tudors and Stuarts. This will include portraits of Henry VIII, Elizabeth I, and Charles I by artists such as Holbein, Van Dyck, and Rubens, royal palaces, printed books, tomb monuments, heraldry, spectacles, as well as portraits of the middle classes. Honors version available.

courses.title: Picture That: History of Photography from Tintypes to Instagram
courses.description: This course presents a select history of photography from its invention to its most recent manifestations. Global in its orientation, this course is designed thematically rather than chronologically to develop dialogues between places and ideas.

courses.title: Art of Exchange and Exploration: Early America and the Globe
courses.description: This course offers a transnational look at American visual culture. It considers the encounters, exchanges, and circulations of art, artists, and ideas across boundaries and oceans from the colonial eighteenth century to the Civil War.

courses.title: Modern Art in Europe 1850-1900: Realism, Impressionism, Post-Impressionism
courses.description: The development of European art from 1850 to 1905, with an emphasis on French avant-garde movements including realism and impressionism, as well as international movements such as symbolism and art nouveau.

courses.title: Picturing Paris: 1800-2000
courses.description: This class explores the cultural, political, and artistic circumstances in which images of Paris have been made and viewed, as well as various visual technologies that have disseminated and marketed.

courses.title: Modern Art in Europe 1900-1960: Avant-Gardes and Politics
courses.description: Major figures, movements, and themes of modernism from cubism and the emergence of abstraction to the transfer of artistic energy and innovation to the United States after World War II.

courses.title: Art Since 1960
courses.description: This course will explore some of the major trends in American and European art, covering a range of provocative objects, ideas, and practices that continue to resonate. It provides a basis for understanding and assessing contemporary art, in relation to various historical, social, cultural, and political contexts. This course presents contemporary art and discourse as diverse, contradictory, contested, and unresolved. Honors version available.

courses.title: African American Art Survey
courses.description: An introduction to African American art and artists and their social contexts from early slavery.

courses.title: Special Topics in Art History
courses.description: Required preparation, any introductory art history course or permission of the instructor. Selected topics in art history.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: Art, Culture, and Power in Africa
courses.description: This course explores how power operates through objects in Africa, including royal regalia, objects used in healing and other ritual contexts, and African art as commodity in international markets.

courses.title: Art History Practicum
courses.description: Students complete an internship in an art history related field. Students will gain practical knowledge of the practice of art history. Studio majors may use this course to fulfill an art history requirement by pursuing faculty-approved, nonpaid internships working in nonprofit or commercial art sectors.

courses.title: Arts of Southern Africa
courses.description: This course focuses on a wide range of regions, time periods, and genres in the visual arts in southern Africa, including archaeological materials, arts associated with longstanding indigenous cultures, art that reflects the often violent encounter with European cultures, and contemporary arts that are produced in the region today.

courses.title: Clothing and Textiles in Africa
courses.description: This class explores how dress reveals information about African aesthetics, culture, and history, including its roles in political systems, religious worship, fashion trends, and other aspects of social life.

courses.title: Arts of West Africa
courses.description: This course addresses the roles of art in the lives of West Africans who make and use it, spanning centuries of African creativity from archaeological sites to 21st-century artists.

courses.title: Art of African Independence
courses.description: This course focuses on African art produced in the mid-twentieth century. It promotes comparative analysis around themes of modernity, nationalism, independence, identity, and the role of the artist in society.

courses.title: Fashioning Identities
courses.description: This course examines fashion and the political, social, and cultural discourses, conditions, and institutional formations used in the creation of varied social and personal identities.

courses.title: Art and Colonialism: France in Africa/Africa in France
courses.description: Art elucidates French and African experiences of colonial rule, as a record of political transformations and a tool for resistance and the assertion of local cultures.

courses.title: Islam and African Art
courses.description: People everywhere use works of art to facilitate worship, to depict spirits, and to celebrate their beliefs. Islam, a major religion in Africa, is no exception. This course focuses on Islam in African visual arts.

courses.title: Loving Your Local Art Scene
courses.description: This course takes students on a tour of Chapel Hill, Carrboro, Durham, and Raleigh's grassroots visual arts scenes, exploring everything from commercial galleries to artist-run non-profits to craft fairs to artists' studios. We will use our local arts scene as a case study to map out how art worlds function. Students' final assignment is to contribute to an ongoing digital web-based - an interactive local arts map. This class is especially beneficial for student artists.

courses.title: From Charlemagne to Bauhaus: German Art and Architecture from the Middle Ages to Modern Time
courses.description: The course focuses on art and architecture in the German-speaking countries (Germany, Switzerland, Austria and in regions formerly belonging to the historical Holy Roman Empire) from Charlemagne in the eighth century to the Bauhaus in the 1920s and beyond. It studies the artistic developments and exchanges with neighboring countries (such as France, Italy, etc.) over the centuries and discusses them in the relevant historical and political contexts.

courses.title: Chinese Landscape Representation in the Second Millennium
courses.description: This course delves into the theme of landscape, or "mountains and waters" (shanshui), which has been a central subject of artistic expression in China since the tenth century. We will explore a selection of landscape paintings from the tenth century through to the early eighteenth century. Students will be introduced to key interpretive approaches for understanding and examining landscapes as both artistic and social entities in pre-modern China.

courses.title: Art, History, and the Modern Museum
courses.description: Focusing on art, history, and ethnography museums in Europe and North America, this course considers the emergence and development of museums as powerful social and cultural institutions from the mid-18th century to the 21st century. A variety of perspectives on museums showcase their connections to larger political and cultural trends.

courses.title: The Art of Dying Well: Death and Commemoration in the Middle Ages and Early Modern Times
courses.description: Covers medieval and early modern artifacts and monuments connected with death as well as the diversity of donations for individual commemoration. Explores the social, political, and economic aspects of medieval/early modern society that affected these developments and phenomena.

courses.title: Saints in Medieval Art
courses.description: This course will explore the modes in which saints and issues related to sainthood are visualized in medieval art.

courses.title: Late Medieval Art
courses.description: This course explores the art of the late medieval period in Byzantium and the Latin West.

courses.title: The Renaissance Portrait
courses.description: This course focuses on European portraits produced in the period c. 1400-1600. Through careful study of specific paintings, prints, and sculptures, by artists such as Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and Albrecht Dürer, we will explore different ways of interpreting portraiture in the Renaissance, addressing issues of identity, reception, and function.

courses.title: European Art and Sexuality
courses.description: Between 1400 and 1600, major European artists (Hieronymus Bosch, Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, Titian, Dürer) made radical contributions to the representation of the sexual body. This course will use Northern European and Italian art as a lens for investigating Early Modern approaches to the figuration of sexuality and gender.

courses.title: Visual Art in the Age of Revolution
courses.description: This course examines the visual culture that participated in revolutions in Europe and the world from circa 1770 to 1850.

courses.title: Life and Art in Ancient Pompeii
courses.description: In this course we will explore the history and archaeology of Pompeii with the goal of better understanding daily life in the early Roman empire. The course proceeds topically, moving from an exploration of the city's public spaces to an analysis of more private domains--houses, gardens, and tombs. We will also consider evidence from ancient literature and epigraphy. Students may not receive credit for both CLAR 380 and CLAS 73.

courses.title: Everything You Ever Wanted to Know About Modern Architecture But Were Afraid to Ask
courses.description: Required preparation, any introductory art history course or permission of the instructor. This course will examine the history of architecture from the early 19th century to the present.

courses.title: Pop Art and Its Legacy
courses.description: This course will investigate what is commonly termed "pop art." We will examine the various issues at stake in the appropriation of mass media imagery and techniques, the diversity within the movement, the different arguments surrounding particular artists and artworks, and pop art's continuing legacy in work by contemporary artists.

courses.title: 20th-Century African American Art
courses.description: Focus on the historical development of African American art from the Harlem Renaissance of early 20th century through the Black Arts Movement and Feminist Art Movement 1960s and early 1970s.

courses.title: Special Topics in Art History
courses.description: Required preparation, any intermediate art history course or permission of the instructor. Selected topics in art history.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: Undergraduate Research Seminar
courses.description: This is the capstone course for art history majors. Required preparation, art history major and junior standing or permission of the instructor. The field and theme of the course change according to the instructor's area of expertise. The seminar introduces students to research in art history and involves an original research project culminating in a substantial research paper.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Directed Readings in Art History
courses.description: Permission of the instructor. Independent study under the direction of a faculty member.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Special Topics in Art History, FC-AESTH
courses.description: Required preparation, any intermediate art history course or permission of the instructor. Selected topics in art history.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: German and Netherlandish Renaissance
courses.description: The course focuses on a crucial period of German and Netherlandish art around 1500, referred to as the so-called Age of Dürer, which still shows influences of Gothic art but also of new Italian Renaissance. Often based on artifacts of the Ackland Art Museum, case studies explore the interaction of artists and patrons in important art centers of the time.

courses.title: Seen, Unseen, and Suggested: Representation and Hollywood Film Censorship
courses.description: This course will look at the history of film censorship in the United States from the perspective of how such things as the Production Code (Hays Code), wartime restrictions, Anti-communist blacklisting, regional and local censorship boards (for example, Southern Baptist Ministers prior to 1968), late 1960s movements for social change, and culturally and socially-determined moral and ethical standards restricted what could and could not be seen on movie screens in American theaters.

courses.title: Constructing Femininity: Women in Chinese Painting
courses.description: This course examines issues of femininity and sexuality in Chinese painting from the Han Dynasty (206 B.C.-220 A.D.) to the end of dynastic China in the nineteenth century. Course topics include the ways in which pictures of women help to craft the notion of femininity in pre-modern Chinese society and the differing roles of women as painters, patronesses, and collectors.

courses.title: The Invention of the Modern Artist
courses.description: This class examines the invention of the idea of the artist in the Western world, starting in Early Modernity and ending with the present. We consider the evolution of the artist's social status, the representation of the artist in a variety of media, shifting expectations for artistic training and community, the relationship between the artist and the art market, and different definitions of artistic genius or excellence in art marking.

courses.title: The City as Monument
courses.description: A city or cities will be considered as cultural artifact(s), with emphasis given to plans and planning, architecture, public monuments and to various institutions, such as religion, government, the arts, and commerce that initiate or affect these urban developments and forms. Honors version available.

courses.title: Women in the Visual Arts II
courses.description: Discussion of topics related to the representation of women in Western art and/or women as producers of art.

courses.title: Africa in the American Imagination
courses.description: Examines the ways African art appears in United States popular culture (advertisements, magazines, toys, films, art) to generate meanings about Africa. Addresses intersecting issues of nationalism, multiculturalism, imperialism, nostalgia, and race. Restricted to sophomores, juniors, and seniors.

courses.title: Cathedrals, Abbeys, Castles: Gothic Art and Architecture, ca.1130-1500
courses.description: Covers the development of Gothic church and secular architecture in Europe between 1130 and 1500. Explores formal and constructive progress in architecture (including sculpture and stained glass windows) and social, political, and economic aspects of medieval society that affected these developments.

courses.title: City, Architecture, Art: Nuremberg as a European Artistic Center,1300-1600
courses.description: The course covers the development of art and architecture from ca. 1300 to ca. 1600 in one of the most important medieval and early modern art centers in Europe: Nuremberg, the hometown of the famous German painter Albrecht Dürer (1471-1528).
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, ARTH 151; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Studies in the History of Graphic Art
courses.description: Required preparation, any intermediate art history course or permission of the instructor. Study of prints and printmaking in Western art from ca. 1400 to the present focusing on selected topics.

courses.title: Greek Sculpture
courses.description: Required preparation, any intermediate art history course or permission of the instructor. A focused study of sculpture in Ancient Greece.

courses.title: Greek Architecture
courses.description: A survey of Greek architectural development from the Bronze Age and Early Iron Age through the fourth century BCE. Special topics include the origins of monumental architecture, the development of the orders and architectural forms, and the role of the built environment in shaping cultural practices in the first millennium BCE.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, CLAR 268, CLAR 375, CLAR 244, or CLAR 492; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Roman Architecture
courses.description: The development of architecture in the Roman world from the ninth century BCE through the fourth century CE. The course focuses on the development of urbanism and the function, significance, and evolution of the main building types and their geographic distribution.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, CLAR 245, CLAR 247, or CLAR/ARTH 263; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: History of the Illuminated Book
courses.description: Chronological survey of major developments in book painting during the European Middle Ages from 300 to 1450 CE.

courses.title: Art of the Aztec Empire
courses.description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the art of the Aztec Empire, including architecture, monumental sculpture, small-scale sculpture, ceramics, painting, lapidary work, gold work, and feather work.

courses.title: Northern European Art of the 14th and 15th Centuries
courses.description: Required preparation, any intermediate art history course or permission of the instructor. Advanced study of painting and sculpture in France, England, and the Netherlands, 1300 to 1400.

courses.title: Early Modern Art, 1400-1750
courses.description: Required preparation, any intermediate art history course or permission of the instructor. This course explores specialized themes and/or broad topics in Western European art of the early modern period. Honors version available.

courses.title: Early Modern and Modern Decorative Arts
courses.description: Required preparation, any intermediate art history course or permission of the instructor. This course traces major historical developments in the decorative and applied arts, landscape design, and material culture of Western society from the Renaissance to the present.

courses.title: Roman Sculpture
courses.description: Survey of Roman sculpture (200 BCE-300 CE), including portraiture, state reliefs, funerary monuments, and idealizing sculpture, with emphasis on style, iconography, and historical development of sculpture in its sociocultural, political, and religious contexts.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, CLAR 245, CLAR 247 or CLAR/ARTH 263; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Roman Painting
courses.description: Surveys Roman painting from 200 BCE to 300 CE, with emphasis on style, iconography, historical development of painting in its sociocultural, political, and religious contexts. Treats current debates in scholarship.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, any CLAR or ARTH course at the 200-level or higher (preferably CLAR 245, CLAR 247, or CLAR/ARTH 263); permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Art and Archaeology of Achaemenid Persia
courses.description: This course will examine the history and material culture of the ancient state known as the Achaemenid Persian Empire through ancient texts and archaeological sources. Beginning in the sixth century BCE, this ancient superpower ruled a vast and culturally diverse empire that stretched from Northern Libya to central Asia. Through an examination of key sites, objects, and texts we will explore the history and diversity of this multicultural empire.

courses.title: Culture on the Move: Art, Empire, and Restitution since 1800
courses.description: This discussion-based course examines the systems of value that confer special status on the broad category of cultural property, then explores a number of case studies of art theft and restitution since the early 19th century, with an emphasis on art theft during World War II and that undertaken under the aegis of European colonialism.

courses.title: Art of the Harlem Renaissance
courses.description: Examines the Harlem Renaissance (1918-1942) as an instance of both transnational modernism and cultural nationalism through study of how artworks articulate interrelated conceptions of race, gender, sexuality, and social class.

courses.title: Contemporary African Art
courses.description: Examines modern and contemporary African art (1940s to the present) for Africans on the continent and abroad. Examines tradition, cultural heritage, colonialism, postcolonialism, local versus global, nationalism, gender, identity, diaspora.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, AAAD 101 or ARTH 152 or 155; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Special Topics in Art History
courses.description: Required preparation, any intermediate art history course or permission of the instructor. Selected topics in art history.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: Monuments and Memory
courses.description: Explores the role of monuments in the formation of cultural memory and identity, both nationally and globally. Topics include the construction of identities in and through public spaces, commemoration of both singular individuals and ordinary citizens, and the appearance of new types of post-traumatic monuments in the 20th century.

courses.title: Introduction to Museum Studies
courses.description: Introduces careers in museums and other cultural institutions. Readings and interactions with museum professionals expose participants to curation, collection management, conservation, exhibition design, administration, publication, educational programming, and fundraising.

courses.title: The Body in Social Theory and Visual Representation
courses.description: A study of how the human body has been represented in contemporary art and the relation of those representations to theories of the individual and society.

courses.title: Urban Africa and Global Mobility
courses.description: The contemporary arts of Africa are framed by urbanization and global mobility. This course examines how artists examine, reflect on, and express visually experiences of these conditions.

courses.title: Art and Money
courses.description: This course explores intersection of art and economics from the 18th century to the present through themes such as value, markets, counterfeiting, and circulation. It examines money as a visual artifact and artworks that engage with monetary questions in the context of art history and Western economic theory.

courses.title: Theories of Modern Art
courses.description: Required preparation, any intermediate art history course or permission of the instructor. A study of theoretical issues central to the understanding of trends in modern art (e.g., modernism, the avant-garde, formalism originality).

courses.title: Cultural Politics in Contemporary Art
courses.description: Permission of the instructor. This course will examine strategies of critique in contemporary art. Organized thematically, it focuses on the tactics employed by artists who address political, social, or cultural issues through their work.

courses.title: Current Issues in Art
courses.description: Addresses select issues that have gained or re-gained prominence in today's art world, for example globalization, training, the market, and the nature of the "contemporary."

courses.title: History and Theory of Museums
courses.description: Required preparation, any intermediate art history course or permission of the instructor. Provides an historical overview of museums. Serves as an introduction to many of the theoretical issues museums face including: ethics, audiences, the role of museums in society, exhibiting dilemmas.

courses.title: Experience in Research
courses.description: Required preparation, one 100-level art history course and one 200- to 399-level art history course. An experiential learning opportunity in independent and original research on a topic or in a field of the student's choosing under the close direction of a faculty supervisor.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Honors in Art History
courses.description: Permission of the instructor. Independent research directed by a faculty member leading to an honors thesis.

courses.title: Honors in Art History
courses.description: Permission of the instructor. Independent research directed by a faculty member leading to an honors thesis.

courses.title: Advanced Readings Topics in the History of Art
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 9 total credits. 3 total completions.

courses.title: Museum Studies Apprenticeship
courses.description: Provides experience in some aspect of museum work: curatorial, educational, collections management, exhibition design, administration. Requires a minimum of 90 hours and will have an academic component.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, ARTH 551 or ARTH 592; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Colonialism and European Visual Culture, 1800-1990
courses.description: Considers the role of visual representation in the construction of European empire and its associated knowledges from the Napoleonic expedition to Egypt to debates over primitivism in the 1980s.

courses.title: Greek Topography
courses.description: Study of chief archaeological sites of Greece and of existing buildings and monuments. Attention to the problems of excavation and the role of the sites in Greek history.

courses.title: Methods in Art Historical Research
courses.description: This course introduces students to a variety of historical and contemporary methods for the interpretation of visual culture.

courses.title: alt-Methods: Digital Art History
courses.description: This course introduces students to current digital art history projects and practices as well as methods for approaching art historical research in new ways.

courses.title: Professional Development
courses.description: This course focuses attention on the variety of ways in which scholars in the arts disseminate their research and market themselves. Students will analyze and participate in various weekly writing and oral exercises, but will focus on one specific genre for their semester long project.

courses.title: Problems in the the History of Art
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 9 total credits. 3 total completions.

courses.title: Seminar in Chinese Art and Architecture
courses.description: Study selected topics in the history of Chinese art and architecture.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Seminar in Contemporary Global Arts
courses.description: This seminar examines contemporary artistic production that engages, questions, and challenges the narratives of culture and art that privilege Europe and America as the models for understanding cultural production.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Seminar in Latin American Art
courses.description: This seminar investigates topics in the history of colonial and modern Latin American Art.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Tudor and Jacobean Portraits: A Theoretical and Practical Investigation
courses.description: This course involves close and critical examination of a select body of extant portraits from the Tudor and Jacobean periods in English history (1485-1625) in the collection of the North Carolina Museum of Art. Students taking this unit will play an active role in researching these relatively unstudied works of art.

courses.title: Mexico City: 1890-1950
courses.description: Permission of the instructor. This course examines the visual culture of Mexico City between 1890 and 1950. It also considers works by artists outside of Mexico who were associated and inspired by cultural production here.

courses.title: Seminar in Contemporary Art
courses.description: Addresses select topics and theoretical issues relevant to contemporary art.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Fashioning Power
courses.description: This graduate seminar focuses on fashion (clothing, accessories, style, performance) as the central cultural component for examining power in society.

courses.title: Seminar in African American Art
courses.description: Advanced standing in art history or permission of the instructor. Explores current debates crucial to the study of African American art. Emphasis on the variety of theories and methods central to the field.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Graduate Writing Seminar
courses.description: Devoted to structuring an argument, assessing primary and secondary sources, and conducting a sustained writing exercise. The goal of the Graduate Writing Seminar is to produce a prospectus of the thesis by the end of the third semester. For Art History graduate students only.

courses.title: Master's Research and Thesis
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Doctoral Research and Dissertation
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: The Artistic Temperament
courses.description: Class examines how to advance and sustain artistic production, focusing not only on being a successful artist, but also on the importance of creativity and hard work in any successful venture. Honors version available.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Time, A Doorway to Visual Expression
courses.description: This class will study one of the lesser considered, but most intriguing, visual components: the element of time.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Stories in Sight: The Narrative Image
courses.description: This class looks at the theory and practice of telling stories through photographs.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: The Visual Culture of Photography
courses.description: This course will investigate how photography is inextricably entwined in our lives and histories.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Please Save This: Exploring Personal Histories through Visual Language
courses.description: This class will investigate the idea of personal histories in visual art. As a studio class, the course will be organized around several art making projects. As a catalyst to our own art making, we will explore the idea of personal history and memory through readings, as well as looking at contemporary artists whose work functions in an autobiographical framework.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Special Topics
courses.description: Content varies by semester.

courses.title: Two-Dimensional Design
courses.description: Studio course investigates concepts and strategies of two-dimensional image making. Introduces design elements of visual language (line, shape, value, texture, color). Considers the cultural codes that accompany visual information and how they combine with organizational structures to determine a variety of effects, influence responses, and inform meaning. Foundation requirement for studio majors.

courses.title: Sculpture : Introduction I (Object/Body)
courses.description: ARTS 103 Sculpture: Introduction I (Object/Body) explores materials, methods, processes, and cultural themes in contemporary sculpture. This project-based course focuses on 3D object investigations, encouraging students to experiment with sculptural techniques, tools, and ideas as a visual language that deepens their understanding of the world through art. Students develop aesthetic sensibility, analytical capacity, and fundamental skills in sculptural media. Foundation requirement for studio majors.

courses.title: Drawing I
courses.description: Working out of an observational tradition, this course provides an introduction to the concepts and techniques of drawing. Paying attention to both representation and interpretation, the course is designed to develop fundamental skills, aesthetic sensibility, analytical capacity, and creative problem-solving in two-dimensional media.

courses.title: Photography I
courses.description: Focusing on creative digital photography, this course provides an introduction to the concepts and techniques of digital imagery and lens-based media. Includes methods of interpretation, analysis of images, scanning, retouching, color correction, basic composition, and inkjet printing. Honors version available.

courses.title: Video I
courses.description: This foundation course introduces students to narrative and non-narrative moving image art through video, sound, and various software programs. Students will learn video production by filming and editing video. Through readings, discussions, screenings, and engagement with artists, projects are designed to develop an understanding of dialogues pertaining to the use of video in contemporary art. Foundation requirement for studio majors.

courses.title: Sonic Arts 1
courses.description: Sound is a physical vibration and an element of perception central to contemporary art, the transmission of information, and our sense of time, place, and space. This interdisciplinary course tunes students toward practices of listening, introduces the fundamentals of audio recording and production in the arts, and engages contemporary sound art and artists working with sound in installation, sculpture, and video. Students will develop sonic literacy by engaging with concepts, artworks, and the material world through the creation of sonic works, site-visits, and reading and discussion activities. Prior experience in sound or music production is not required.

courses.title: Darkroom Photography I
courses.description: Introduction to black and white photography in the darkroom through photograms, pinhole, and SLR cameras, processing film, and making gelatin silver prints. Concepts are developed through making, reading and writing, engaging with established and historical artists, and critiquing peers' work. B&W process and aesthetic is approached as tradition, genre, abstraction.

courses.title: Graphic Design as a Tool for Art-making
courses.description: This course introduces students to the essential principles and practices of graphic design while developing technical proficiency in industry-standard digital tools. Students will learn to create content from various digital platforms, then transform their digital work into tangible forms through various physical production methods including inkjet printing, vinyl cutting, router and/or laser cutting. Through hands-on projects such as stencil design, wood objects, flag design, banners, and experimental zines-students will master fundamental design concepts such as vector graphics, comprehension of visual hierarchy, layout design, typography principles, color theory, and visual communication.

courses.title: Collage: Strategies for Thinking and Making
courses.description: Collage is both an artistic technique and a way of thinking. Even though its historical roots stem from the early 20th century, it is an image-construction strategy that is almost ubiquitous today. Using a variety of conceptual and media approaches, this course explores strategies of collage in contemporary studio practice.

courses.title: Digital Drawing I
courses.description: This class delves into the convergence of traditional drawing and technology by harnessing the capabilities of powerful drawing apps like Adobe Fresco and others, utilizing the graphic tablet as a primary tool to replicate natural mediums. Beyond technical proficiency, the course critically examines how new media perpetually influences traditional studio practices, providing valuable insights into contemporary methods of artistic production. Please note that the class exclusively covers iPad versions of drawing applications, excluding mobile apps like Procreate for iPad or Clip Studio for Android. Owning a personal iPad is not a prerequisite for enrollment.

courses.title: Painting I
courses.description: Recommended preparation, ARTS 104. This course will introduce the fundamentals of painting and various painting techniques through studio lab activity, lectures, demonstrations, and discussions. The course intends to guide students through developing their technical, formal, conceptual, and creative sensibilities to the painting process.

courses.title: Sculpture II
courses.description: An expansion on the foundations of three-dimensional artwork as taught in Sculpture I. Students will continue the research and 3D art making through materials, process and context through the application of the various sculpture media.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, ARTS 103; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Photography II
courses.description: Continuation of ARTS 105 with continued focus on advanced creative digital photography techniques.

courses.title: Video II
courses.description: In this intermediate-level class students expand on video production skills including lighting techniques, blocking and staging, and sound recording. Students learn advanced post production skills including sound design, color grading and further develop skills in continuity editing and non-narrative forms. Students will deepen their creative process and artistic strategies through research and writing to develop projects, and learn how to work collaboratively.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, ARTS 106; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Sonic Arts 2
courses.description: This intermediate-level course builds upon the foundations of audio recording and production introduced in Sonic Arts 1. Students will expand their sonic literacy through advanced production and post-production practices, including mixing for various spaces, creating multi-channel sound installations, and working with specialized microphones such as hydrophones and contact microphones. The course introduces electrocrafting as a means of exploring non-conventional forms of audio generation and transmission. Through case studies, readings, and discussions, students will refine their creative processes and critical engagement with contemporary arts, culminating in a capstone project that integrates sound and visual or sculptural mediums.

courses.title: Print I
courses.description: Introduction to four basic approaches to printmaking: intaglio, relief, planographic, and stencil processes. Students will explore creative strategies unique to the printed process.

courses.title: 2D Animation
courses.description: This class explores several techniques of 2D character animation, including storyboarding and conceptualizing, pencil testing and timing animation, animating simple sequences with Photoshop, experimenting with coloring and materials under a film camera, and compositing in After Effects.

courses.title: Ceramic I
courses.description: An investigation of clay as a medium; developing technical skills, aesthetic awareness, and historical perspective.

courses.title: Life Drawing
courses.description: Through the study of anatomy and observation of the human form, students develop the ability to create powerful, realistic figure drawings. Fundamental skills and concepts include expressive use of line, value, weight, and volume plus classical techniques in shading, gesture, sighting, and composition.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, ARTS 104; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Darkroom Photography II
courses.description: Continuation of ARTS 115 with advanced focus on conceptual topics and techniques of black and white analog photography. This course will provide students with proficiency in the operation of medium and large format cameras and advanced printing techniques. Concepts are developed through making, reading and writing, engaging with established and historical artists, and critiquing peers' work.

courses.title: Color: Theory and Concept
courses.description: This course explores the intricacies of color theory with regard to perception, systems, and application in visual art. Further, the course considers color as subject and concept in contemporary art. Previously offered as ARTS 121.

courses.title: Wood Sculpture
courses.description: This class examines wood sculpture from both a technical and intuitive perspective. Students are taught woodworking skills and are then encouraged to use these skills to discover their creative potential.

courses.title: Screen Printing
courses.description: Recommended preparation, Any Tier I Studio Art course. An intermediate studio course focused on creating stencil-based print images. Students explore a range of technical approaches and will investigate art making concepts specific to screen printing as well as the intersections of screen printing with other two-dimensional art forms.

courses.title: Metal Sculpture
courses.description: This class examines metal sculpture from both a technical and intuitive perspective. Students are taught metalworking skills and are then encouraged to use these skills to discover their creative potential.

courses.title: Special Topics in Studio Art
courses.description: Required preparation, any introductory studio art course or permission of the instructor. Selected topics in studio art.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: Painting II
courses.description: This course aims to continue guiding painting students through developing sensibilities to paint handling, color, composition, and spatial design, with an emphasis on experimentation. Students will develop their work in context to themes that are significant in painting history, relevant to contemporary art, and their personal lens.

courses.title: Loving Your Local Art Scene
courses.description: This course takes students on a tour of Chapel Hill, Carrboro, Durham, and Raleigh's grassroots visual arts scenes, exploring everything from commercial galleries to artist-run non-profits to craft fairs to artists' studios. We will use our local arts scene as a case study to map out how art worlds function. Students' final assignment is to contribute to an ongoing digital web-based - an interactive local arts map. This class is especially beneficial for student artists.

courses.title: Ceramic II
courses.description: Continuation of ARTS 213.

courses.title: Narrative Painting
courses.description: Students will explore themes in the vast history of narrative paintings by researching and responding to these themes, and create narrative paintings through their own personal lens. We will explore topics of the genre, from historical works, to how contemporary artists are interpreting and creating narratives that mirror the diverse spectrum of identities, materials, and histories in our lifetime.

courses.title: Sculpture Garden: Art in the Public and Projects of Scale
courses.description: Sculpture Garden is a theme-based course taught through a faculty-led project as a way to develop interdisciplinary student-centered approaches to large scale/public artworks on campus and beyond. The course is centered on the Alumni Sculpture Garden as a locus for understanding space, place, and large scale contemporary art. Coursework reflects the intellectual and professional missions and research-creations of our faculty, collaboratively engaging these skill sets, from ideation to execution in projects and research presentation of scale.

courses.title: Drawing II
courses.description: This class builds on predominantly perceptually based concepts of basic drawing and introduces abstraction, interpretive, and conceptual drawing strategies. Class assignments develop understanding of the language of drawing and provide a foundation that aims to support independent investigation and personal approaches to drawing's unique capabilities.

courses.title: MAKE: Art in the (New) Age
courses.description: Suggested preparation, ARTS 103. This course examines the connecting trajectories of artistic and technological developments from early modernism to the contemporary. While addressing the interconnected nature of technology, technique, craft and art, students will work with our new technologies (Laser and Vinyl Cutter, 3D Printer, etc.) to create 3D work.

courses.title: Abstract Painting
courses.description: This studio course will explore the vast visual language of abstract painting. Students will examine abstraction through creating paintings within a historical, visual, and cultural framework, and acquire context about the emergence and persistence of painted abstraction.

courses.title: Phantasmagoria: Haunted Art, History, and Installation
courses.description: This course will be organized around four art making/art building projects, culminating in a class presentation of a multimedia phantasmagoria. Students will research early light/shadow, pre-cinema techniques, hauntings/horror and artists whose work is influenced by these tropes. We will work with Maker's Spaces to produce components for this course. Previously offered as ARTS 253.

courses.title: The Practice of Representation: Portraiture in Photography
courses.description: This course examines the practical and theoretical issues of portraiture. Students will learn technical skills and conceptual strategies to engage with issues of representation and notions of identity. We will explore the history of the photographic portraiture as well as work of contemporary portrait artists working in a post-modern age.

courses.title: Letterpress
courses.description: This class explores the concepts and craft of letterpress printing. Technical skills include typesetting, linoleum carving, and digital interfaces for making image and text matrices. Projects explore the special relationship of image and word and are designed around specific text/image forms: broadside, poster, portfolio, and book.

courses.title: At the Radical Edge of Life: Art, Space, and Ecology
courses.description: Art at the Edge of Life: Art, Space, and Ecology is a course organized around 2-3 art making/art building projects, culminating in a class presentation of a final public art installation. Part seminar and part studio, students will research early ecology, sustainability, green movements and artists whose work is influenced by these tropes. We will work with BeAM and with experts in the field to find solutions for the issues that we face today.

courses.title: The Walking Seminar: A Territorial Investigation
courses.description: Recommended preparation, ARTS 104. This seminar engages students in a territorial investigation of the North Carolina landscape. Meandering through the landscape we will explore different art mediums while simultaneously fostering an appreciation for the natural environment. Through hiking and backpacking students will foster a means for understanding their location and documenting their experience.

courses.title: Print II
courses.description: This course continues an investigation of print techniques and concepts. Projects develop an understanding of print strategies, focusing on the affordances of processes unique to printmaking. This approach positions traditional techniques as a point of departure for seeking an expanded definition of printmaking.

courses.title: Art, Rites and Rituals of Pilgrimage
courses.description: This course is an introduction to the culture, history and contemporary context of pilgrimage and the Camino de Santiago through the lens of performance art and other embodied aesthetic experiences. Several performative projects form the core of the coursework with the Camino de Santiago-specifically, the Camino Francés, becomes the site and our studio for both cultural and artistic purposes.

courses.title: States of Change
courses.description: This course will investigate the idea of a lived practice. As a class in studio arts, the course is organized around several perspectives on what it means to be rooted in social engagement. As a catalyst to our own art making and understanding of our mediums and fields, we will explore the proximity of art and social action and the utility of social engagement through service-learning projects set in the global landscape.

courses.title: Special Topics in Studio Art
courses.description: Required preparation, any intermediate studio art course or permission of the instructor. Selected topics in studio art.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: Advanced Painting Projects
courses.description: This course focuses on the historically rich practice of painting, and is designed to guide the advanced painting student through the research, conceptual, aesthetic, and technical components of a comprehensive studio practice, and developing and maintaining a studio work ethic.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, ARTS 302, 322, or 352; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Art and Science: Merging Printmaking and Biology
courses.description: This class explores the intersection of two disciplines, art and science. Research skills intrinsic to both include curiosity, close observation, experimentation, and visual analysis. Organized around printmaking projects informed by specific topics in biology, students adapt theory and practical skills from both disciplines to create artworks using several printmaking techniques. Permission of the instructors. Honors version available.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, a 200-level BIOL course or a 200-level ARTS course, and permission of the instructor; Corequisite, BIOL 409L.

courses.title: Advanced Ceramic Projects
courses.description: Continuation of ARTS 313. May be repeated for credit.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, ARTS 313; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Performance as Social Practice: Exploring Artistic Expression and Social Change
courses.description: This course introduces the politics of performance art and its implications on social practice. Through a blend of seminar discussions, group workshops, and critique sessions, we will delve into various strategies for engaging with the medium. Our exploration will involve careful consideration of decolonial gestures, materiality, space, context, and intentionality. We'll analyze how contemporary artists navigate discourses surrounding race, gender, sexuality, nationality, and class. Active participation in reading discussions, exercises, and artist lectures is mandatory.

courses.title: Conceptual-Experimental Photography
courses.description: An advanced photography course for students interested in contemporary photographic practices, critical theory, art history, and experimental processes: theory and practice, formal and conceptual investigations, and historical and contemporary strategies will all be given equal attention.

courses.title: Advanced Video
courses.description: This advanced level video course focuses on the conceptual development of long-term projects with a focus on advanced production skills. Students will continue to deepen their production and post-production skills through in class tutorials while expanding upon experimental and non-narrative artistic strategies such as multi-channel installation.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, ARTS 106, ARTS 206; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Advanced Mixed Media Projects
courses.description: Cultural production and practice, theory, and criticism. Pursuit of individual visual projects, formally and conceptually, through theoretical, poetic, art historical, and autobiographical texts, critiques, collaboration, and discussion using all media.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Advanced Printmaking
courses.description: This course is appropriate for students who have had a minimum of three semesters of prior printmaking experience. Students submit a proposal outlining technical and artistic goals for the semester.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, ARTS 208 and any two of ARTS 238, 338, or 348; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisites.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Book Art
courses.description: Required preparation, one additional two-dimensional studio course (drawing, photography, or printmaking). Defining the book as a "multiple and sequential picture plane," this course considers a range of traditional approaches and conceptual departures of the book as a format for creative expression.

courses.title: Photo Printmaking
courses.description: This course combines a technical approach (making printing matrices using photographic processes) with a conceptual framework (the photographic "voice" and its interpretation in printmaking). Artmaking projects explore salient ideas such as appropriation versus capture, documentation, truth-telling and fabrication, or narrative invention using specific technical processes such as photogravure and cyanotype.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, ARTS 105 and 208; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisites.

courses.title: Advanced Special Topics in Studio Art
courses.description: Required preparation, any intermediate studio art course or permission of the instructor. Advanced consideration of selected topics in studio art.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: Studio Art Practicum or Internship
courses.description: Required preparation, 15 hours ARTS courses. Allows studio art majors to pursue unpaid practicums or internships for credit. Examples include working as a studio assistant or working in art-related fields, such as galleries, design firms, architectural firms, and nonprofit arts organizations. Work undertaken must comply with Federal criteria governing unpaid internships. Departmental approval required.

courses.title: Senior Professional Practices Seminar
courses.description: This course is a capstone course for the studio art major. Appropriate for BFA students and BA students who anticipate careers in fine art and art adjacent fields (e.g. design.) Topics covered include issues of professional development, curatorial practice, and presentation of works of art in exhibition. The culminating project is mounting the Senior Exhibition. Restricted to senior studio art majors.

courses.title: Advanced Topics in Photography
courses.description: May be repeated for credit.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, ARTS 205 or 215; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Independent Study in Studio Art
courses.description: Permission of the instructor. For students wishing to pursue additional media or thematic study beyond the advanced level. Students register with section numbers designated for faculty. May be repeated for credit.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: Movie Making Machines: Learning About Cinema in the Maker Space
courses.description: This projects-based seminar will introduce students to the fundamental optical and technological principles of motion pictures. By using the Maker Space to design and fabricate pinhole cameras, zoetropes, and 16mm film strips, students will gain a deep understanding of the material and technological foundations of the cinema, and the operating principles that are behind not only the classic films of Hollywood's past, but the high-definition digital imaging technologies of the present.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, ARTS 105, 106, 209, or COMM 130; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Advanced Topics in Studio Art
courses.description: Required preparation, any intermediate studio art course or permission of the instructor. Selected topics in studio art.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 3 total credits. 1 total completions.

courses.title: Senior Honors Thesis Project in Studio Art
courses.description: Permission of the department. ARTS 691H is designed to enable studio art majors to pursue serious and substantial work. In addition to working with the instructor of record for ARTS 499/691H, students work under the supervision of an individual thesis advisor and committee.

courses.title: Senior Honors Thesis Project in Studio Art
courses.description: ARTS 692H is taught concurrently with and by the instructor for ARTS 500. In addition to the classroom component, students continue to work with an individual thesis advisor and committee. Successful completion of ARTS 692H allows students to graduate with honors or highest honors.

courses.title: Graduate Studio Art Seminar
courses.description: Graduate Studio Art Seminar.

courses.title: Teaching Practicum
courses.description: Teaching Practicum

courses.title: Qualifying Review
courses.description: Qualifying Review.

courses.title: M.F.A. Graduate Group Critique
courses.description: M.F.A. candidates meet weekly for organized group analysis and critique of their art work. Each candidate presents work on rotating basis before a panel of faculty and peers.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: Master's Project in Studio Art
courses.description: Master's Project in Studio Art.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: The Samurai: Gender and Power in Japanese History
courses.description: Examines the history of the samurai, the hereditary, elite warrior population that emerged as a new social and political force in Japan in the 12th century and which ruled, largely unchallenged, until the Meiji Restoration of 1868. In the modern era, frequent reinventions situated the samurai as core to understanding ''traditional'' Japan, as well as vague and aphoristic notions of the Japanese spirit and Japanese masculinity.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Food in Chinese Culture
courses.description: Examines the cultural practice and meanings of food, cooking, eating, and drinking through Chinese literature and cinema. Main themes include food and rituals, gourmandism and poetic taste, cannibalism and the grotesque, and hunger and revolution.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Kung-Fu: The Concept of Heroism in Chinese Culture
courses.description: Film, history, novels, and theater are used to explore the rich, complex kung-fu tradition in Chinese culture from ancient to modern times, as well as its appropriation in foreign films.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Writing Women in Modern China
courses.description: Compares the rhetoric of equality between the sexes presented by late Qing, May Fourth, and communist thinkers to perspectives on gender and society by 20th-century Chinese women writers. Honors version available.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Dis-Orienting the Orient
courses.description: Examines how the East is constructed as the Orient in different historical periods: 19th-century European colonialism, 1950s to 1960s Hollywood films, contemporary Japanese animation, and the global war on terrorism.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Media Masala: Popular Music, TV, and the Internet in Modern India and Pakistan
courses.description: Explores different examples of broadcast and digital media (music videos, soap operas and reality shows, radio, and social media) with respect to history, gender, sexuality, globalization, environment, religion, regionalism, and activism.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Israeli Culture and Society: Collective Memories and Fragmented Identities
courses.description: The course explores selected themes and case studies pertinent to culture and society in modern Israel, with emphasis on debates about "Israeliness" in various cultural and social arenas.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: A Tour of South Asia's Regional Art Cinemas
courses.description: Students watch and analyze art films by filmmakers working in various languages and regions of South Asia. Students are introduced to the aesthetics and themes that have shaped the various regional cinemas of South Asia. Course materials introduce students to some of the formal elements of filmmaking and provide cultural and historical context.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Philosophy on Bamboo: Rethinking Early Chinese Thought
courses.description: This course will introduce students to the main works and themes in early Chinese thought from the earliest recorded writings down to the Qin unification in 221 BCE.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Wars and Veterans: Iran, Iraq, and Afghanistan
courses.description: In this seminar, we will explore the various ways that Iran-Iraq, United States-Iraq, and United States-Afghanistan wars have been portrayed in literature, film, and photography. We will deepen and enrich our understanding of war experienced by both veterans and civilians. We will also read articles on war criticism and psychology.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Asia in Iberian Converso Literature, 1500s-1650s
courses.description: This course examines how 16th- and 17th-century Iberian authors of Jewish heritage imagined and represented Chinese, Filipinos, Japanese, and Indonesians in their writings (e.g. plays, historical narratives, economic treatises, travel accounts, maps, etc.). We explore how these authors' representations of Asians not only dialogued with various interwoven variables (political, economic, and religious factors), but also revealed the historically complex issue regarding notions of personal identities and nationhood.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Transnational Korea: Literature, Film, and Popular Culture
courses.description: This first-year seminar introduces students to the history of transnational imaginations in modern Korea. Using literature, film, and television, it explores the ways in which Korean cultural producers have used narratives of transnational travel and exchange to rethink Korea's place in the world and refashion the bounds of Korean identity.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Popular Culture in the Arab World
courses.description: This first-year seminar introduces students to aspects of popular culture in the Arab world, taking it as an entry point for understanding the histories, cultures, and societies of the region. The course relies on anthropological readings alongside direct engagements with examples of popular culture from the Arab world.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Imagining Palestine
courses.description: This course explores the idea of Palestine as in Palestinian creative works. We will study what Palestine is for Palestinians, how Palestinian relationships to and expectations of Palestine have changed over time; and how Palestinian portrayals of their homeland have affected perceptions of Palestine/Israel and the Arab world. How have art, film, and literature shaped Palestinian identities and aspirations throughout modern Palestinian history? How have they contributed to personal agency?

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Love in China
courses.description: We all know that love is not easy. But what makes it so complicated? This course examines how the conception of ''love'' in Chinese culture offers a key to understanding emotions, family structure, gender and sexuality, consumer desire, as well as political sentiments. We will probe into these issues through literary and visual materials from the 8th century B.C.E. to the 21st century.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Traveling to China and Traveling from China in the Premodern World
courses.description: Reading records written by various travelers - merchants, missionaries, pilgrims, nomads, and diplomats - this course examines cross-cultural and transregional interactions premodern Chinese had with the broader world through the lens of travel. In addition to reading and discussion, students will create digital itinerary maps based on the primary sources.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Women and Performance in Transnational Asia
courses.description: This course examines art and activist performances produced by women in transnational and global Asia, which speak of their feminist, post-colonial, and anti-hegemonic agenda. These performances reveal various nations' struggle to globalize and reflect how the category of "Asian," intersected with gender, continues to evolve in the West. This course engages with these performances theoretically and responds to the artists' strong voices with critical analysis.

courses.title: First Year Seminar: Special Topics
courses.description: Special topics course. Content will vary each semester. Honors version available.

courses.title: Iranian Post-1979 Cinema
courses.description: We examine the ways the medium has been used to incorporate political and social perspectives, challenge the government, and document the lives and struggles of Iranian people. Among the topics explored are Iranian culture and society, gender politics, ethnicity, attitudes about religion, role of children, and various schools of realism. Previously offered as ASIA 224.

courses.title: Transnational Lives: Culture, Film, and Fiction in the Iranian and Indian Diasporas
courses.description: This course explores the lives of Iranian and South Asian diasporic communities with a focus on the cultures of migration, and their representation in cinematic and literary narratives. Engaging with the disciplines of ethnography, film studies, and literary analysis, this course evaluates various research methodologies, giving students tools to approach the diasporic experience from multiple vantage points. Students will examine how migration and transnationalism shape cultural identity, social narratives, and artistic expression, paying special attention to the ways in which diasporic communities negotiate belonging and adaptation in host societies like the United States.

courses.title: Introduction to Persian Literature
courses.description: This course introduces students to Persian literature from classical to contemporary writers in translation to help them understand the efforts of the Iranian literati in addressing issues surrounding love, the sacred, human diversity, inclusiveness, and the rise of the modern nation-state in Iran through the use of literature.

courses.title: Iranian Women Writers
courses.description: This course introduces students to Iranian women's issues through their literary works. To contextualize, we will read articles and essays on the historical, cultural, social, political, and economic backgrounds. In order to approach these literary works in a more effective manner, we will also be reading various secondary materials.

courses.title: Southeast Asia before 1800 through Digital History
courses.description: This course will cover the history of the territories and peoples of Southeast Asia (comprising the modern-day countries of Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Thailand, Timor-Leste, Singapore and Vietnam), from earliest times to 1800. The course will also delve into debates about the past, who is engaged in such debates, and how to navigate these debates to find reliable historical sources and communicate analysis of those sources for a wide audience.

courses.title: Modern Southeast Asia
courses.description: The history of Southeast Asia from the 19th century to the present. Long-term political, economic, social, and intellectual questions, including the impact of imperialism, the rise of nationalism, the transformation of the economy, the Cold War, and the coherence of Southeast Asia as a region.

courses.title: Introduction to Chinese History
courses.description: Chinese history from its beginnings to the present, organized around the central theme of how the identity of China and 'Chineseness' was created.

courses.title: Modern East Asia
courses.description: Comparative and interdisciplinary introduction to China, Korea, and Japan in the 19th and 20th centuries, focusing on impact of the West, nation building, industrialization, and evolution of mass society.

courses.title: History of the Indian Subcontinent to 1750
courses.description: An introduction to major political, religious, social, and cultural events from 3500 BCE to 1750 CE with a focus on Hindu, Muslim, and Buddhist groups before British colonial rule.

courses.title: History of India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh: South Asia since 1750
courses.description: This course is an introduction to modern India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. We will investigate major political, social, economic, and cultural issues from 1750 to the present.

courses.title: History of Muslim Societies to 1500
courses.description: A broad, comprehensive, and interdisciplinary introduction to the traditional civilization of the Muslim world. Students may not receive credit for both HIST 138/ASIA 138 and ASIA 180/RELI 180.

courses.title: History of Muslim Societies since 1500
