courses.description: This course offers an introduction to the history and practice of East Asian martial arts. We will explore the social, political, and cultural contexts of the martial arts, from the classical period to the present. Integral to this course is a practical component involving embodied experience with martial arts training.

courses.title: Special Topics in Communication Study
courses.description: A special topics course on a selected aspect of communication studies.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Internships
courses.description: Permission of the department. Majors only. 2.5 cumulative grade point average required. Individualized study closely supervised by a faculty advisor and by the departmental coordinator of internships. Cannot count toward the COMM major.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Media, Culture, and the Environment
courses.description: This research-based course is framed by two broad questions: What does science tell us about the natural and changing environments? How do politics and popular culture interpret and present this crisis?

courses.title: Independent Study and Directed Research
courses.description: Permission of the department. Majors only. 3.0 cumulative grade point average and 3.5 communication studies grade point average required. For communication studies majors who wish to pursue independent research projects or reading programs under the supervision of a selected instructor. Intensive individual research on a problem designed by instructor and student in conference.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Critical Theory
courses.description: An introduction to European modern and contemporary philosophy, from the enlightenment to contemporary postmodernism.

courses.title: Family Communication
courses.description: Growth in technologies, more frequent travel, and movements of products and people across the borders of nation states change concepts of family and community. Foregrounded by these realities, this course combines theories of family and communication with documentation of lived experience to interrogate family communication patterns in contemporary culture. Honors version available.

courses.title: Critical Perspectives on Work, Labor, and Professional Life
courses.description: This upper level seminar develops a critical perspective on work, labor, and professional life within the global context. Throughout, we will engage in moral and philosophical debates about the status of labor and the meanings of work in our daily lives.

courses.title: Communication and Community Work
courses.description: Together, APPLES Service-Learning & Communication Beyond Carolina will let us learn deeply how to be in community well with others. This course requires 30 hours of service beyond the classroom and the ability to travel to a school in Orange County. The ideals of community are often utopian and high-minded. The work of community is often small, steady, consistent, and scrappy. This semester we use our in-class time to examine the communication basis of communication and community ideals, and examine how those ideas intersect with our semester-long experience of serving as a community member in a local school.

courses.title: History of American Screenwriting
courses.description: This viewing and research-intensive course examines the history of American narrative film through the screenwriter's experience, using a decade-by-decade approach to examine the political, social, global, psychological, religious, and cultural influences on the art, process, and careers of screenwriters.

courses.title: Advanced Audio Production
courses.description: Advanced analysis and application of the principles and methods of audio production.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 130 or 150; Grade of C or better in COMM 130; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Visual Culture
courses.description: Course provides an overview of theories of visual culture. We apply these theories to better understand contemporary visual media and technologies, along with the everyday media practices they support.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 140 or COMM 249; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Intermediate Screenwriting
courses.description: Open only to students in the writing for the screen and stage minor. Conceiving and outlining a feature-length screenplay.

courses.title: TV Structure and Genre
courses.description: This course approaches TV structure and genre from a screenwriter's point of view. Through weekly screenings and writing exercises, students learn to analyze episodic storylines and story beats, and to recognize the "genre goods" for eight different TV genres.

courses.title: Memory Acts
courses.description: Advanced introduction to foundational work in memory and performance studies, emphasizing theory and practice of various forms of remembering. Honors version available.

courses.title: United States Black Culture and Performance
courses.description: Examines how the United States Black experience is constituted in and through performance across a range of cultural contexts including the antebellum South, Reconstruction, the Harlem Renaissance, the Black Aesthetic, and contemporary urban life.

courses.title: Media and Popular Culture
courses.description: Examination of communication processes and cultural significance of film, television, and other electronic media. Permission of the instructor for nonmajors.

courses.title: The History of New Media Technology in Everyday Life
courses.description: The starting point for this course, chronologically and conceptually, is the emergence of popular media technology. Our purview includes transformative innovations in mediated communication, such as telephony and e-mail, alongside familiar media technologies such as televisions and computers.

courses.title: Media and Activism
courses.description: A study of the electronic media as a feedback mechanism for community organization and social change. A variety of broadcast and nonbroadcast uses of the media are studied.

courses.title: Sound Studies
courses.description: This course is about sound and the auditory dimension. In a society dominated by images and spectacle, sound and listening have been remarkably under-appreciated. Sound is physical-the vibration of molecules according to frequencies, pitches, and intensities-and biological-our ability to hear is an evolutionary trait. But sound is also cultural (what qualifies as signal or noise?), technological (how is sound recorded and reproduced?), and historical (how has the soundscape changed and how have we listened differently).
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 140 or COMM 249; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Creating the Solo Performance
courses.description: This course examines processes of creating and performing solo work. Students engage a variety of performances: autobiographical, representation of the lives of other/s, and exploration of cultural or political ideas.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 160, DRAM 120, or ENGL 206, 207, or 208; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Collaborative Performance
courses.description: Theory and practice of collaborative performance, emphasizing image, intertextual adaptation, site-specific and installation work, avant-garde traditions, and the play of time and space. Honors version available.

courses.title: Advanced Study in Performing Literature
courses.description: This course engages the theory and embodiment of prose fiction, poetry, and other kinds of literary texts, including nonfiction. Students practice adaptation and script preparation, solo/group performance, and performance critique.

courses.title: Political Communication and the Public Sphere
courses.description: A course covering the relationship between communication and political processes and institutions. Topics include media coverage and portrayal of political institutions, elections, actors, and media influence on political beliefs.

courses.title: Rhetorics of Public Memory
courses.description: Takes up the fundamental assumptions of contemporary memory studies and the centrality of rhetoric to memory. Research focus on how constructions of the past respond to the present and future.

courses.title: Rhetorical Criticism
courses.description: Approaches to the analysis and assessment of rhetorical practice with a focus on how rhetoric reflects and shapes public culture.

courses.title: Advanced Public Speaking: Speaking in Community
courses.description: This course provides hands-on experience in public communication, focusing on real-world impact within the Chapel Hill community. In partnership with a local nonprofit dedicated to youth mentorship, students will use their public speaking skills to increase awareness of the organization's mission and support recruitment efforts for new mentors. Through this collaboration, students will explore the structural challenges facing the local community, develop tailored communication strategies, and create deliverables to enhance the nonprofit's outreach. In addition to preparing public presentations, students will represent the nonprofit in public speaking engagements, gaining practical experience in advocacy and community engagement.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 113 or COMM 223; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Fostering Civil Discourse: Reasoning Together for Common Good
courses.description: People are finding it increasingly difficult to reason with anyone outside their political affiliations. Must that be the case? This course is founded on the belief that democratic participation begins with earnest conversation and, given the right tools, we can do democracy better. The course is committed to the promise of shared reasoning and aims to foster student capacities for robust deliberative practices, rooted in the rhetorical tradition and tackling the most challenging public issues.

courses.title: Special Topics in Communication Studies
courses.description: Permission of the instructor for nonmajors. A special topics course on a selected aspect of communication studies.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: The Dark Side of Interpersonal Communication
courses.description: The "dark side" of communication is a metaphor describing the study of disruptive, dysfunctional, distorted, distressing, and destructive aspects of communication. This course explores humanity's darker side that allows us to reject, exclude, stigmatize, exploit, objectify, misguide, lie, and cheat. The course examines various theoretical perspectives and applies them to everyday problems in interpersonal encounters. A sample of topics discussed include: prejudice, stigma, marginalization, bullying, ostracism, resistance, manipulation, conformity, deceit, gossip, rumors, infidelity, and revenge.

courses.title: Visual and Material Rhetoric
courses.description: This course explores the use of rhetorical criticism as a way to understand how the visual and material are used for symbolic and political purposes. Examples ranging from news images to public art will be studied.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 170 or permission of the instructor.

courses.title: Communication and Social Memory
courses.description: Permission of the instructor for nonmajors. An investigation of psychological aspects of communication, particularly the perceptual and interpretive processes underlying the sending and receiving of messages.

courses.title: Communication and Leadership
courses.description: Critical examination of alternative theories of leadership and trends in the study of leadership; focuses on the communicative dimensions of leadership. Permission of the instructor for nonmajors.

courses.title: Gender, Communication, and Culture
courses.description: Course examines the speeches and other texts that announced and embodied the goals and political strategies of multiple branches of three waves of feminist activism in the United States.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 224; permission of the instructor for non-majors.

courses.title: Organizational Communication
courses.description: Permission of the instructor for nonmajors. Provides a critical exploration of organizational communication theory, research, and application, examining the factors involved in the functioning and analysis of complex organizations.

courses.title: Critical-Cultural Approaches to Organizational Communication
courses.description: The study of organizational culture operates on a set of assumptions distinct from traditional management perspectives. This course explores the cultural perspective as an alternative approach to understanding organizational communication processes.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 325; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Organizational Ethics
courses.description: A critical examination of the theory, research, and practice of organizational ethics.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 325 or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Performing the Screenplay
courses.description: Introduces students to approaches for creating performance from screenplays and other texts for electronic media forms, focusing on scripts as literature and the tensions between live and electronically delivered performances.

courses.title: Aesthetic and Technical Considerations in Making Short Videos
courses.description: The course examines the aesthetic and technical elements at work and play in cinematic storytelling. The student is required to complete three projects and will gain hands-on experience in narrative filmmaking.

courses.title: Introduction to Screen Adaptation
courses.description: Students practice the craft of screen adaptation by conceptualizing, outlining, and writing scenes based on material from another medium (both fiction and nonfiction). Work is presented, discussed, and performed in a workshop environment.

courses.title: Master Screenwriting
courses.description: Open only to students in the writing for the screen and stage minor. Students will write and workshop a full-length feature film screenplay. Students will learn about the film and television business through a combination of research, in-class discussions, and interactive interviews with industry insiders.

courses.title: Sexuality and Visual Culture
courses.description: Examines questions about sexuality and how it has changed over time, through various media of visual communication.

courses.title: Performance of Women of Color
courses.description: Explores through performance contemporary poetry, fiction, nonfiction, and feminist thought by women of color in the United States. Honors version available.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 160 or COMM 260 or COMM 263.

courses.title: Oral History and Performance
courses.description: This course combines readings and field work in oral history with the study of performance as a means of interpreting and conveying oral history texts. Honors version available.

courses.title: Performance and Popular Culture
courses.description: Critical examination of the operation of performance as a cultural phenomenon, with an emphasis on meaning, power, and resistance in cultural events, social practices, and media spectacles.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 160 or COMM 260 or COMM 263.

courses.title: Adapting and Directing for the Stage
courses.description: This course introduces students to practices in adapting and directing literary texts for live ensemble performance. Students will create original performance work, engage in collaborative critique, and discuss the development of aesthetic value.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 160 or COMM 260 or COMM 263.

courses.title: Rhetorical Theory and Practice
courses.description: Investigates the theoretical definitions and uses of rhetorical interpretation and action in spoken, written, visual, material practices, discourses, and events.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 170 or permission of the instructor.

courses.title: Public Policy Argument
courses.description: Analyzes argument in a variety of contexts with an emphasis on public policy and exploring tensions involved in addressing both expert and public audience in the political sphere.

courses.title: The American Experience in Rhetoric
courses.description: Examines public discourse from the colonial period to the present. Discourses, critical perspectives, and historical periods studied will vary.

courses.title: War and Culture
courses.description: Examines American cultural myths about war generally and specifically about the causes of war, enemies, weapons, and warriors, and the way these myths constrain foreign and defense policy, military strategy, and procurement.

courses.title: Presidential Rhetoric
courses.description: The power of the presidency depends in part upon the president's ability to rally public opinion, which depends upon the president's ability to use the "bully pulpit." This course examines the hurdles presidents face and the steps presidents take to shape opinion.

courses.title: Race and Rhetoric
courses.description: This course examines the role of symbols, speech, and trope in the invention of race, the perpetuation of racism, and anti-racist resistance through a historical, global, and intersectional lens. The course provides an introduction to rhetorical scholarship on topics such as the voices and vernaculars of marginalized communities, cultural and political racial representations, and racialized public discourse linked to borders and national identity. The course investigates topics through case studies tied to subjects such as social movements, branding, entertainment industries, protests, economic crises, presidential speeches, court cases, legislation, fashion, debate, standup comedy, documentaries, scientific inquiry, and digital media.

courses.title: Rhetoric and Black Culture
courses.description: This course will explore the complex ways in which Black aesthetic forms and creative expression function as public discourse.

courses.title: Advanced Independent Study/Directed Reading
courses.description: Permission of the department. Majors only. 3.0 cumulative grade point average and 3.5 communication studies grade point average required. For the communication studies major who wishes to pursue an advanced independent research project under the supervision of a selected instructor. Intensive individual research on a problem designed by instructor and student in conference.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Screenwriting: The Re-Write
courses.description: This course is designed to take the completed feature screenplay written in COMM 537 and prepare the re-written final draft for production companies and agencies. It will begin with a complete structural review, character analysis, and dialog polish. A logline, synopsis and one sheet shall be developed. Critical analysis will be given, received, and addressed, resulting in a final screenplay package that is prepared to be submitted to professionals. Students must be in WSS program.

courses.title: Theories of Interpersonal Communication
courses.description: Permission of the instructor for nonmajors. Course focuses on how communication is used to build and sustain interpersonal relationships. Forms and functions of communication are examined as a means of testing and defining relationships.

courses.title: Hate Speech
courses.description: The primary focus of hate speech is on the ways that interactants manipulate hatred to accomplish a variety of social and personal goals. The pursuit of this focus will allow the student to appreciate the operation of hatred in a variety of contexts. Often taught as a service-learning course.

courses.title: Communication and Nonprofits in the Global Context
courses.description: Introduces students to the opportunities, challenges, and rewards of participation within the nonprofit/NGO sector. The course also equips students with the skills needed to design and conduct engaged scholarship.

courses.title: Documentary Production
courses.description: A workshop in the production of video and/or film nonfiction or documentary projects. The course will focus on narrative, representational, and aesthetic strategies of documentary production.

courses.title: Interactive Media
courses.description: Explores interactive media through creative projects that include sound, video, and graphic elements. Technical information will serve the broader goal of understanding the aesthetics and critical issues of interactive media.

courses.title: Game Design
courses.description: Permission of the instructor for nonmajors. Studio course that explores gaming critically and aesthetically. Practice in game design and production including 3-D worlds and scripting.

courses.title: Game Studio
courses.description: Game Studio is a project-based course in the new media track. This course is designed to provide a structured environment, instructor and peer feedback, along with technical and conceptual resources in which to complete a new media project. Students may work individually or on collaborative teams. The class focuses on idea development, design, and experimentation.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 638; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Special Topics in Cultural Studies
courses.description: Permission of the instructor for nonmajors. This course will explore various specific topics, theories, and methodologies in cultural studies.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Documentary Production: First Person Filmmaking
courses.description: Students create documentaries emphasizing the filmmaker's personal perspective and experience: essay, diary, and autobiographical films, and pieces in which the filmmaker performs a role for expressive or political ends. Significant class time is devoted to work-shopping student films.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 230; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: The Documentary Idea
courses.description: Historical and theoretical examination of expressions of the documentary idea in different eras and various modes including film, television, and radio. Permission of the instructor for nonmajors.

courses.title: Introduction to the Art and Mechanics of Two-Dimensional Digital Animation
courses.description: Students use Adobe After-Effects and Adobe Photoshop as their primary image software to create several original animations. Assignments are given weekly, and a substantial final project is expected.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 130 or 150; Grade of C or better required in COMM 130.

courses.title: Advanced Projects in Media Production
courses.description: Recommended preparation, several production courses above COMM 230. Course provides a structured environment, instructor and peer feedback, along with production and postproduction resources for completing advanced near-to-graduation media projects. Projects can be narrative, documentary, experimental, or interactive.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMM 230 and one of COMM 534, 635, 646, 653, or 654.

courses.title: Cultural Politics of Global Media Economies
courses.description: Primary subjects will be popular culture and media technology, and guiding questions will be organized around the relationships of each to commerce and/as social change.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 140 or COMM 249; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Media and Difference
courses.description: This course examines critical and theoretical issues concerning the representation and study of various modes of difference, such as sexuality, race, and gender, in specific media texts. Permission of the instructor for nonmajors.

courses.title: Experimental Video
courses.description: This course allows students to create video productions that play with forms that lie outside of mainstream media.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 230; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Motion Graphics, Special Effects, and Compositing
courses.description: In this course students learn a wide range of video post production techniques working mostly with the application After Effects.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 130 or 150; Grade of C or better in COMM 130; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Television Culture
courses.description: This course introduces students to critical television studies. The course emphasizes not television or culture as separate entities but instead "Television Culture." The focus of the class is on the interrelationship between television and contemporary culture.

courses.title: Sound for Film and Video: Theory and Practice for Motion Picture Sound Design
courses.description: The aim of this course is to provide students who have an interest in film and video production with an understanding of the technical, conceptual, and aesthetic implications of the motion picture soundtrack, with a special emphasis on sound-image relationships. Students who have already developed a basic proficiency in the use of video cameras, audio recorders, and editing software will be asked to cultivate an understanding of and appreciation for the expressive and artistic possibilities.

courses.title: Movie Making Machines: Learning About Cinema in the Maker Space
courses.description: This projects-based seminar will introduce students to the fundamental optical and technological principles of motion pictures. By using the Maker Space to design and fabricate pinhole cameras, zoetropes, and 16mm film strips, students will gain a deep understanding of the material and technological foundations of the cinema, and the operating principles that are behind not only the classic films of Hollywood's past, but the high-definition digital imaging technologies of the present.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, ARTS 105, 106, 209, or COMM 130; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Surveillance Cultures
courses.description: We live in surveillance societies. Just about every element of our lives is affected by surveillance: workplaces and schools, social media sites and mobile phone use, police encounters and security screening. Surveillance practices shape how institutions operate and how people see themselves and others. The goal of this course is to develop a critical awareness of surveillance and its implications for society.

courses.title: Advanced Projects in Performance Studies
courses.description: Course provides a workshop setting for the process of creation, dramaturgy, development, analysis, and critique of graduates' and undergraduates' original performance work, focusing on the needs of each project in progress.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 160 or COMM 260 or COMM 263.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Race and Ethnicity
courses.description: Examines race and ethnicity in specific geopolitical contexts as discursive formations, performative identities, and lived realities. Studies disciplinary/political boundaries that are produced and maintained through acts of performance.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 160 or COMM 260 or COMM 263.

courses.title: Black/African Diaspora Performance
courses.description: Recommended preparation, COMM 160. Relying on critical race theories, colonial and postcolonial theories, and theories of performance, this course engages comparative discourses of Black/African diaspora citizenship through the literature, poetry, fiction, nonfiction, drama, and cultural performances of people of African descent, particularly in Africa, Europe, and the Americas.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 160 or COMM 260 or COMM 263.

courses.title: Performance, Politics, and Culture
courses.description: This course is a arts-based inquiry into the ways in which performance and theatricality structure contemporary politics, culture, and everyday life, as well as the ways in which artists utilize performance as mode of political engagement.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 160, COMM 260, COMM 262, or COMM 263.

courses.title: Media in Performance
courses.description: Required preparation, one performance studies course above COMM 400. Permission of the instructor for students lacking the required preparation. Project-based class where students acquire skills and critical approaches to create collaborative, professional, multimedia works.

courses.title: Performance Activism
courses.description: History and practice of performance in contemporary social movements. Practical exploration of direct action, guerilla theatre, and performance interventions.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 160 or COMM 260 or COMM 263.

courses.title: Digital Media and Live Performance
courses.description: Permission of the instructor for undergraduates. Intended for students from various majors, this course provides a foundation in the history, theory, and practice of developing live, technologically-intensive, multimedia performance works. The course analyzes new media masterworks, addresses techniques of interdisciplinary collaboration, and offers workshops in specific software/technology applications.

courses.title: Contemporary Film Theory
courses.description: Overview of poststructuralist, or "contemporary" film theory. Traces its development, its techniques, fierce critiques lobbed at it since the early 1980s, and its points of continuing importance.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, ARTH 159, COMM 140, or ENGL 142; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: History of the Moving Image: Pasts, Presents, Futures
courses.description: Theories of moving images and imaging technologies--from the primitive to the not-yet-existing--that focus on their multifaceted relations with various registers of time, memory, flux, and futurity.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, ARTH 159, COMM 140, or ENGL 142; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Advanced Topics in Communication Studies
courses.description: Permission of the instructor for nonmajors. A special topics course on a selected aspect of communication studies. May be repeated. Honors version available.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Honors in Cultural Studies
courses.description: Permission of the instructor. Required of all senior honors candidates in cultural studies. First semester of senior honors thesis.

courses.title: Honors in Cultural Studies
courses.description: Permission of the instructor. Required of all senior honors candidates in cultural studies. Second semester of senior honors thesis.

courses.title: Honors
courses.description: Permission of the department. Majors only. Cumulative grade point average must meet University standard. Individual projects designed by students and supervised by a faculty member.

courses.title: Honors
courses.description: Permission of the department. Majors only. Cumulative grade point average must meet University standard. Individual projects designed by students and supervised by a faculty member.

courses.title: Field Methods
courses.description: Recommended preparation, COMM 562 or 841. A bridge course designed to offer graduate students and advanced undergraduates a practicum in fieldwork methods and performance ethnography.

courses.title: Introduction to Modern Philosophy and Contemporary Theory
courses.description: Considers the emergence of modern and contemporary social and cultural theory. Surveys major paradigms of modern and contemporary philosophy.

courses.title: Introduction to Research and Theory in Communication Studies II
courses.description: Admission to graduate program or permission of the department. Considers theory and philosophy in the study of communication. Surveys major paradigms of contemporary social/cultural theory (and their roots in modern philosophy) in relation to examples of communication research and practice. Second of two semesters.

courses.title: Teaching in Communication Studies
courses.description: Communication studies graduate students only. An introduction to teaching at the university level for new teaching assistants and graduate students hoping to have teaching-related responsibilities in communication studies. It is designed to encourage us to have intellectually rigorous and personally meaningful conversations about our teaching.

courses.title: Communication and the Political
courses.description: This course is designed for students to start thinking, in a historical and foundational way, about 'the political' as defined by formative thinkers from contrasting philosophical perspectives, as well as from necessarily different social positions within the field of power.

courses.title: Communication and Discourse
courses.description: This course focuses on the various ways that the problem of discourse is rendered inside and outside of Communication Studies. It examines the various modes at our disposal for thinking about discourse as a field of articulation: for example in theories of representation, mediation, and meaning making.

courses.title: Communication and the Social
courses.description: This class theorizes the Social by drawing on resources inside and outside of communication studies, thinking through the implicit and explicit investments that communication scholarship has in the concept of the social.

courses.title: Performance as Method
courses.description: Course introduces graduate students to performance practice as a way of knowing, an aesthetic expression, a form of pedagogy, a method of research, and a means of presenting findings. Students will develop and perform original work that creatively engages various research contexts.

courses.title: The Body and Performance
courses.description: This course will explore through performance the various ways the human body is 'marked' or signified in culture.

courses.title: Primary Readings in Performance Studies
courses.description: Course introduces graduate students to key texts that have informed the emergence of Performance Studies as a mode of inquiry into cultural, social, aesthetic, and political practices.

courses.title: Research in Organizational Communication
courses.description: Explores theoretical, methodological, and practical issues encountered in ethnographic, case study, and field research on communication phenomena in organizations.

courses.title: Feminism, Science, and Communication
courses.description: Critical examination of key feminist arguments about science and communication scholarship as conventionally defined; exploration of alternative goals, assumptions, and practices for research consistent with feminist theories and methodologies.

courses.title: Interpretive Studies in Organizational Communication
courses.description: Focuses on the theory and practice of interpretive organizational communication research, including organizational phenomena such as culture, metaphor, symbolism, ritual, and narrative.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 525; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Critical Studies in Organizational Communication
courses.description: Focuses on the theory and practice of critical organizational communication research, including organizational phenomena such as power, discourse, and culture.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 525; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Cultural Studies
courses.description: Graduate standing required. Introduction for graduate students to the current literature and critical perspectives in the areas of media and cultural studies.

courses.title: Media and Social Change
courses.description: This seminar inquires into the range of relationships between media and social life, with a particular emphasis on media's role in movements for social, economic, and/or cultural transformation.

courses.title: Theories of the Audience/Public
courses.description: This course offers a sustained analysis of the ways in which the media, audience, and/or public have been variously conceptualized historically, in critical theory.

courses.title: Political, Institutional, and Economic Contexts of Media and Culture
courses.description: A detailed analysis of the relationship between government, policy making, corporate and business interests, and various theoretical approaches to their impact on media and culture. Fall.

courses.title: History of Cultural Studies
courses.description: This class introduces cultural studies through its British 'origins,' especially but not only the work of the Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies and the Open University.

courses.title: National, International, Transnational, and Global Movie/Media History
courses.description: Explores the economic, social, ideological, technological, and aesthetic development of film and television as international, transnational, transcultural, and global entities, questioning the viability of the concept of national cinema/media in the 21st century.

courses.title: Studies in Film and Television
courses.description: Graduate introduction to the study of film, television, and video. This course traces the theoretical and methodological development of media studies.

courses.title: Adaptation Seminar
courses.description: This seminar recognizes and applies narrative theory in understanding texts, lives, and cultural practice broadly.

courses.title: Topics in Performance Studies
courses.description: Second-year graduate students and/or permission of the instructor. Special problems in performance studies.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: History of Rhetoric I
courses.description: A critical survey of the history of rhetoric, focusing on Classical theories of rhetoric from Greece and Rome through the Medieval period.

courses.title: History of Rhetoric II
courses.description: A critical survey of the history of rhetoric, focusing on theories of rhetoric from the Renaissance through the 19th century.

courses.title: Seminar in Contemporary Rhetorical Theory
courses.description: A critical survey of the history of rhetoric focusing on rhetorical theory from the 20th century to the present.

courses.title: Visual and Material Rhetorics
courses.description: Addresses conceptual and practical issues in the rhetorical analysis and criticism of visual and material objects, practices, and events.

courses.title: Seminar in Kenneth Burke
courses.description: Seminar is an in-depth analysis of the writings of Kenneth Burke, concentrating on primary source materials.

courses.title: Philosophy of Communication and Culture
courses.description: Considers the history of and developments in the philosophy of communication and culture, as well as the role these concepts have played in western philosophy.

courses.title: Topics in Research Methods
courses.description: Advanced study of selected topics in research methods. Topics vary.

courses.title: Rhetorical Criticism
courses.description: Investigates the function of rhetorical criticism, the critical method, and a variety of approaches to the performance of rhetorical criticism.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMM 571; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Practicum in Rhetorical Criticism
courses.description: Focuses on practice in writing rhetorical criticism and on mid-range theoretical concepts that inform critical analysis and argument.

courses.title: Technology, Culture, & Power
courses.description: This graduate seminar will serve as an advanced introduction to critical studies of modern technological systems. Drawing upon the fields of communication studies, science and technology studies, cultural studies, geography, anthropology, sociology, and gender studies, seminar participants will investigate the role of technologies in shaping social worlds and producing political orders. Attention will be given to the social construction of technological systems, the politics of mediation and resistance, and the encodings of power relations.

courses.title: Critical Ethnic Studies (CES): New Perspectives
courses.description: This course is devised to provide graduate students interested in theoretical interdisciplinary work with a sense of prevailing questions and critiques important to CES. CES takes on the more difficult questions of intersectional work, as it thinks through sovereignty and emancipation, identity and ontology, place, space and temporality. Each iteration of the course works itself through new perspectives in the field, challenging students to create new methodologies for their own work.

courses.title: Seminar in Family Communication
courses.description: This course is an advanced seminar in which students may study family communication and produce original research.

courses.title: Seminar in Feminist Studies in Communication
courses.description: This course compares and critically evaluates the work of major feminist scholars in the field of communication. Spring.

courses.title: Seminar in Interpersonal and Organizational Communication
courses.description: A variable topic seminar that permits faculty and graduate students the opportunity to explore significant historical and emerging issues in the field of communication.

courses.title: Performance Ethnography
courses.description: This seminar focuses on methods of ethnography and fieldwork ethics. Performance as theory and practice informs methodological inquiries as well as the analysis of specific ethnographic texts and case studies.

courses.title: Seminar in Performance and Cultural Studies
courses.description: This course focuses on performance-related issues in the emergent field of cultural studies.

courses.title: Seminar in Contemporary Performance Theory
courses.description: An advanced graduate seminar, this course will address recent developments and problems in performance theory. It will consider cross- and multidisciplinary approaches to performance as sites for consideration and debate.

courses.title: Seminar in Performance and History
courses.description: This course explores diverse relations among performance and history, including the performance of life histories, the use of spectacle in history, everyday performances of historical protocols, and performance itself as an historical construct.

courses.title: The Political Economy of Performance
courses.description: This course examines social relations, particularly power relations, by focusing on resistance as performance and the performance of resistance arising from the dynamics and conflicts within specific locations of a political economy.

courses.title: Performance Pedagogy
courses.description: Draped in the political, economic, and domestic histories of western culture our current pedagogies still point out the world that matters to each new generation. We will study these pedagogies from the perspectives of institutions, economies, and human relationships they simultaneously reflect and work to transform.

courses.title: Seminar in Culture and Identity
courses.description: This course looks at issues of the representation and production of identity, subjectivity, and agency - in various forms - in the practices of media.

courses.title: Seminar in Media Studies
courses.description: Selected problems in media aesthetics. Exact topic to be covered is announced before classes begin.

courses.title: Research Methods in Media and Cultural Studies
courses.description: Graduate standing required. Introduction to the issues, methods, and materials of research in media and cultural studies.

courses.title: Seminar in the History of Media
courses.description: Application of historical research techniques to problems in the mass media. Exact topic is announced before classes begin. May be repeated.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Seminar in Popular Culture
courses.description: This course will look at special topics in the study of popular culture. Designed for advanced graduate studies, it will consider critical responses to existing scholarship with original research.

courses.title: Seminar in Media Difference
courses.description: This seminar explores critical theories of difference and puts them into dialogue with media representations of difference.

courses.title: Seminar in Cultural Studies
courses.description: This class explores the impact of some developments in postmodernism - as an interpretive, historical, and philosophical discourse on the possible development of cultural studies.

courses.title: Seminar in Communication Technology
courses.description: Examines new communication technologies, their spatial and social diffusion, and how these relate to theories of culture, politics, and technology and the real-world contexts in which technologies are received. May be repeated.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Seminar in Cultural Studies and Popular Culture
courses.description: This course will focus on specific topics, issues, or queries of popular culture as these have been or can be studied within cultural studies.

courses.title: Seminar in Feminist Studies of Film and Television
courses.description: Graduate standing required. This graduate seminar explores theoretical and practical points of contact between feminism, film, and television using psychoanalysis, narrative analysis, ideological analysis, and cultural studies.

courses.title: Seminar in Media and Cultural Studies
courses.description: This course, designed for advanced graduate students, will explore specialized topics in interpretive, critical, and cultural research in media studies.

courses.title: Aesthetics and Communication
courses.description: Explores how theories of aesthetics have struggled with notions of beauty, value, pleasure, and pain in the human communicative experience.

courses.title: Rhetoric and Black Culture
courses.description: This course will examine the manner in which Black aesthetic and intellectual expressions and controversies function as public discourse in cultural politics.

courses.title: Rhetorics of Space and Place
courses.description: Considers place in relation to space and time. Primary concentration on implications of theorizing place as communicative practice rather than communicative context.

courses.title: Rhetoric and Public Memory
courses.description: Addresses the fundamentally rhetorical character of public memory. Analyzes theoretical presuppositions about memory. Openings for rhetorizing memory.

courses.title: Topics in Rhetorical and Cultural Studies
courses.description: Special problems in rhetorical and cultural studies. May be repeated.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics.

courses.title: Research Practicum
courses.description: Permission of the internship coordinator. Individualized practical experience supervised by a faculty advisor and by the departmental coordinator of internships. May be repeated.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics.

courses.title: Directed Research
courses.description: Permission of the instructor. Individual research on a problem defined by the graduate student and graduate faculty member in conference. May be repeated.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics.

courses.title: Research Practicum in Communication Studies
courses.description: Individualized practical research.

courses.title: Proseminar in Professional Development
courses.description: This course advances graduate students' exposure to academic resources and common norms, practices, and procedures related to academic professionalism in Communication Studies.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 2 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Master's (Non-Thesis)
courses.description: Focuses on the development of a master's project or a major paper other than a thesis.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Master's Research and Thesis
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Doctoral Research and Dissertation
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Everyday Computing
courses.description: The goal of this first-year seminar is to understand the use of computing technology in our daily activities. In this course, we will study various examples of how computing solves problems in different aspects in our daily life. Honors version available.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Robotics with LEGO®
courses.description: This seminar explores the process of design and the nature of computers by designing, building, and programming LEGO robots. Competitions to evaluate various robots are generally held at the middle and at the end of the semester. Previous programming experience is not required. Honors version available.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Folding, from Paper to Proteins
courses.description: Explore the art of origami, the science of protein, and the mathematics of robotics through lectures, discussions, and projects involving artistic folding, mathematical puzzles, scientific exploration, and research. Honors version available.

courses.title: First -Year Seminar: Special Topics
courses.description: Special topics course. Content will vary each semester. Honors version available.

courses.title: Introduction to Programming
courses.description: Introduces students to programming from a computational perspective. With an emphasis on modern applications in society, students gain experience with problem decomposition, algorithms for data analysis, abstraction design, and ethics in computing. No prior programming experience expected. Foundational concepts include data types, sequences, boolean logic, control flow, functions/methods, recursion, classes/objects, input/output, and data organization and transformations. Students may not enroll in COMP 110 after receiving credit for COMP 210. Honors version available.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, A C or better in one of the following courses: MATH 130, 152, 210, 231, 129P, or PHIL 155, or STOR 120, 151, 155.

courses.title: Introduction to Scientific Programming
courses.description: An introduction to programming for computationally oriented scientists. Fundamental programming skills, typically using MATLAB or Python. Problem analysis and algorithm design with examples drawn from simple numerical and discrete problems.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, A grade of C or better in one of the following courses: MATH 130, 152, 210, 231, 129P, or PHIL 155, or STOR 120, 151, 155.

courses.title: Practical Web Design and Development for Everyone
courses.description: A ground-up introduction to current principles, standards, and best practice in website design, usability, accessibility, development, and management through project-based skills development in HTML5, CSS, and basic JavaScript. Intended for nonmajors.

courses.title: Topics in Computing
courses.description: Special topics in computing targeted primarily for students with no computer science background. This course has variable content and may be taken multiple times for credit. As the content will vary with each offering, there are no set requisites but permission from instructor is required.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: Data Structures and Analysis
courses.description: This course will teach you how to organize the data used in computer programs so that manipulation of that data can be done efficiently on large problems and large data instances. Rather than learning to use the data structures found in the libraries of programming languages, you will be learning how those libraries are constructed, and why the items that are included in them are there (and why some are excluded).
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 110 and MATH 231; a grade of C or better is required; Pre- or corequisites, COMP 283 or MATH 381 or STOR 315.

courses.title: Systems Fundamentals
courses.description: Systems programming fundamentals including data representation, pointers, execution models, memory management, and runtime environments. Process model, input/output, and system calls. Lexical analysis, parsing, interpretation, and translation. Command-line interface tools including shell, editor, compiler, linker, test harness, debugger, version control, and build tooling. The overarching goal is to bridge the gap between a students' knowledge of a high-level programming language (COMP 110, 210) and computer organization (COMP 311).
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMP 210; COMP 283 or MATH 381 or STOR 315; a grade of C or better is required in both prerequisite courses.

courses.title: ACM Programming Competition Practice
courses.description: Structured practice to develop and refine programming skills in preparation for the ACM programming competition.

courses.title: Effective Peer Teaching in Computer Science
courses.description: Fundamentals of computer science pedagogy and instructional practice with primary focus on training undergraduate learning assistants for computer science courses. Emphasis on awareness of social identity in learning, active learning in the computer science classroom, and effective mentorship. All students must be granted a computer science learning assistantship or obtain prior approval to substitute relevant practicum experience prior to enrollment.

courses.title: Discrete Structures
courses.description: Introduces discrete structures (sets, tuples, relations, functions, graphs, trees) and the formal mathematics (logic, proof, induction) used to establish their properties and those of algorithms that work with them. Develops problem-solving skills through puzzles and applications central to computer science. Honors version available.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, MATH 231 or MATH 241; a grade of C or better is required.

courses.title: Special Topics in Computer Science
courses.description: Non-technical topics in computer science for computer science majors. May not be used to satisfy any degree requirements for a computer science major. This course has variable content and may be taken multiple times for credit.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 4 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: Internship in Computer Science
courses.description: Computer science majors only. A signed learning contract is required before a student may register. Work experience in non-elementary computer science. Permission of instructor and director of undergraduate studies required.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, MATH 231 or 241; COMP 210, COMP 211, and COMP 301; a grade of C or better is required in COMP 210, 211, and 301.

courses.title: Foundations of Programming
courses.description: Students will learn how to reason about how their code is structured, identify whether a given structure is effective in a given context, and look at ways of organizing units of code that support larger programs. In a nutshell, the primary goal of the course is to equip students with tools and techniques that will help them not only in later courses in the major but also in their careers afterwards.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMP 210; COMP 283 or MATH 381 or STOR 315; a grade of C or better is required in both prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Computer Organization
courses.description: Introduction to computer organization and design. Students will be introduced to the conceptual design of a basic microprocessor, along with assembly programming. The course includes fundamental concepts such as binary numbers, binary arithmetic, and representing information as well as instructions. Students learn to program in assembly (i.e., machine) language. The course covers the fundamentals of computer hardware design, transistors and logic gates, progressing through basic combinational and sequential components, culminating in the conceptual design CPU.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMP 211; a grade of C or better is required.

courses.title: Technology, Ethics, & Culture
courses.description: This discussion-based, participatory course explores the personal, sociocultural, and ethical effects and implications of the development and use of computing technologies and the Internet. Honors version available.

courses.title: The Internet: Studies and Stories
courses.description: An interdisciplinary look at historical, social, cultural, ethical, psychological and other dimensions of the Internet through the lenses of works in Internet studies and science fiction. Students design and lead class sessions, conduct and present on research, and create digital art and artifacts.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMP 380; a grade of C or better is required.

courses.title: Computer Science Elective Topics
courses.description: Elective topics in computer science for computer science majors. May not be used to satisfy any degree requirements for a computer science major. This course has variable content and may be taken multiple times for credit.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: Software Engineering Practicum
courses.description: Students develop a software program for a real client under the supervision of a faculty member. Projects may be proposed by the student but must have real users. Course is intended for students desiring practical experiences in software engineering but lacking the experience required for external opportunities. Majors only.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 211 and 301, or COMP 401, 410, and 411; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 6 total completions.

courses.title: Foundation of Programming
courses.description: Required preparation, a first formal course in computer programming (e.g., COMP 110, COMP 116). Advanced programming: object-oriented design, classes, interfaces, packages, inheritance, delegation, observers, MVC (model view controller), exceptions, assertions. Students may not receive credit for this course after receiving credit for COMP 301. Honors version available.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, MATH 231 or MATH 241; a grade of C or better is required.

courses.title: Data Structures
courses.description: The analysis of data structures and their associated algorithms. Abstract data types, lists, stacks, queues, trees, and graphs. Sorting, searching, hashing. Students may not receive credit for this course after receiving credit for COMP 210.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, MATH 231 or 241, and COMP 401; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Computer Organization
courses.description: Digital logic, circuit components. Data representation, computer architecture and implementation, assembly language programming. Students may not receive credit for this course after receiving credit for COMP 311.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, MATH 231 or 241,and COMP 401; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Files and Databases
courses.description: Placement of data on secondary storage. File organization. Database history, practice, major models, system structure and design. Previously offered as COMP 521.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 210, 211, and 301; or COMP 401, 410, and 411; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Foundations of Software Engineering
courses.description: This course introduces students to the fundamentals of Software Engineering. Students gain experience with design thinking and processes, technical communication, team collaboration, project management methodology, the software development lifecycle, and more, with an emphasis on today's best industrial practices.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, C or better in both COMP 211 and COMP 301.

courses.title: Modern Web Programming
courses.description: Developing applications for the World Wide Web including both client-side and server-side programming. Emphasis on Model-View-Controller architecture, AJAX, RESTful Web services, and database interaction.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 211 and 301; or COMP 401 and 410; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Internet Services and Protocols
courses.description: Application-level protocols HTTP, SMTP, FTP, transport protocols TCP and UDP, and the network-level protocol IP. Internet architecture, naming, addressing, routing, and DNS. Sockets programming. Physical-layer technologies. Ethernet, ATM, and wireless.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 210, 211, and 301; or COMP 401, 410, and 411; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Mobile Computing Systems
courses.description: Principles of mobile applications, mobile OS, mobile networks, and embedded sensor systems. Coursework includes programming assignments, reading from recent research literature, and a semester long project on a mobile computing platform (e.g., Android, Arduino, iOS, etc.).
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 210, 211, and 301; or COMP 401, 410, and 411; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Computer Security Concepts
courses.description: Introduction to topics in computer security including confidentiality, integrity, availability, authentication policies, basic cryptography and cryptographic protocols, ethics, and privacy. A student may not receive credit for this course after receiving credit for COMP 535.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 210, 211, and 301; or COMP 401, 410, and 411; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Privacy Enhancing Technologies
courses.description: Covers fundamental tools and technologies designed to protect digital privacy, including what we understand digital privacy to mean with an emphasis on cryptographic techniques for building privacy-preserving systems.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMP 301; a C or better in all prerequisites required.

courses.title: Quantum Computing
courses.description: Recommended preparation, some knowledge of basic linear algebra. An introduction to quantum computing. Basic math and quantum mechanics necessary to understand the operation of quantum bits. Quantum gates, circuits, and algorithms, including Shor's algorithm for factoring and Grover's search algorithm. Entanglement and error correction. Quantum encryption, annealing, and simulation. Brief discussion of technologies.

courses.title: Models of Languages and Computation
courses.description: Introduction to the theory of computation. Finite automata, regular languages, pushdown automata, context-free languages, and Turing machines. Undecidable problems.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 210 or 410 and COMP 283 or MATH 381 or STOR 315; a grade of C or better in all prerequisite courses is required.

courses.title: 2D Computer Graphics
courses.description: Fundamentals of modern software 2D graphics; geometric primitives, scan conversion, clipping, transformations, compositing, texture sampling. Advanced topics may include gradients, antialiasing, filtering, parametric curves, and geometric stroking.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 210, 211, and 301; or COMP 401, 410, and 411; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Applications of Natural Language Processing
courses.description: Natural language processing (NLP) uses mathematics, machine learning, linguistics, and computer science to make language computationally accessible and analyzable. In this course, you will learn to do essential NLP tasks using Python and survey a selection of NLP applications to describe the problems or tasks each addresses, the materials and methods used, and how the applications are evaluated. At least a semester of Python or equivalent practical experience is highly recommended.

courses.title: Information Retrieval
courses.description: Study of information retrieval and question answering techniques, including document classification, retrieval and evaluation techniques, handling of large data collections, and the use of feedback.

courses.title: Data Science in the Business World
courses.description: Business and Computer Science students join forces in this course to create data-driven business insights. We transgress the data science pipeline using cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and real-world datasets. Students acquire hands-on skills in acquiring data, wrangling vast unstructured data, building advanced models, and telling compelling stories with data that managers can understand.

courses.title: Mentored Research in Computer Science
courses.description: Independent research conducted under the direct mentorship of a computer science faculty member. If repeated, the repeated course can not be counted for the major. For computer science majors only. Permission of instructor required.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Independent Study in Computer Science
courses.description: Permission of the department. Computer science majors only. For advanced majors in computer science who wish to conduct an independent study or research project with a faculty supervisor. May be taken repeatedly for up to a total of six credit hours.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Special Topics in Computer Science, FC-CREATE
courses.description: This course has variable content and may be taken multiple times for credit. Different sections may be taken in the same semester.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: Compilers
courses.description: Design and construction of compilers. Theory and pragmatics of lexical, syntactic, and semantic analysis. Interpretation. Code generation for a modern architecture. Run-time environments. Includes a large compiler implementation project.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 301, 311, and 455 or COMP 410, 411, and 455; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Software Engineering Laboratory
courses.description: Organization and scheduling of software engineering projects, structured programming, and design. Each team designs, codes, and debugs program components and synthesizes them into a tested, documented program product.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 301 and 311; as well as at least two chosen from COMP 421, 423, 426, 431, 433, 520, 530, 535, 575, 580, 590.

courses.title: Programming Language Concepts
courses.description: Concepts of high-level programming and their realization in specific languages. Data types, scope, control structures, procedural abstraction, classes, concurrency. Run-time implementation.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMP 301 or COMP 401; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Operating Systems
courses.description: Types of operating systems. Concurrent programming. Management of storage, processes, devices. Scheduling, protection. Case study. Course includes a programming laboratory. Honors version available.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 301 and 311; or COMP 401, 410, and 411; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Distributed Systems and Concurrent Programming
courses.description: Design, implementation, and performance of abstractions for creating concurrent and distributed programs, and use of these abstractions to support high performance computing and distributed, fault-tolerant consistency.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMP 301; a grade of C or better is required.

courses.title: Introduction to Computer Security
courses.description: Principles of securing the creation, storage, and transmission of data and ensuring its integrity, confidentiality and availability. Topics include access control, cryptography and cryptographic protocols, network security, and online privacy.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 301 and 311; or COMP 401, 410, and 411; as well as COMP 550, and COMP 283 or MATH 381 or STOR 315; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisites.

courses.title: Cryptography
courses.description: Introduces both the applied and theoretical sides of cryptography. Main focus will be on the inner workings of cryptographic primitives and how to use them correctly. Begins with standard cryptographic tools such as symmetric and public-key encryption, message authentication, key exchange, and digital signatures before moving on to more advanced topics. Potential advanced topics include elliptic curves, post-quantum cryptography, and zero-knowledge proofs. Honors version available.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 211 and COMP 301; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisites.

courses.title: Digital Logic and Computer Design
courses.description: This course is an introduction to digital logic as well as the structure and electronic design of modern processors. Students will implement a working computer during the laboratory sessions.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 301 and 311; or COMP 401, 410, and 411; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Programming Intelligent Physical Systems
courses.description: Introduction to programming embedded control systems that lie at the heart of robots, drones, and autonomous vehicles. Topics will include modeling physical systems, designing feedback controllers, timing analysis of embedded systems and software, software implementations of controllers on distributed embedded platforms and their verification. Honors version available.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 301 and COMP 311; or COMP 411; a C or better is required in all pre-requisites.

courses.title: Algorithms and Analysis
courses.description: Formal specification and verification of programs. Techniques of algorithm analysis. Problem-solving paradigms. Survey of selected algorithms.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 211 and 301; or COMP 410; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Bioalgorithms
courses.description: Bioinformatics algorithms. Topics include DNA restriction mapping, finding regulatory motifs, genome rearrangements, sequence alignments, gene prediction, graph algorithms, DNA sequencing, protein sequencing, combinatorial pattern matching, approximate pattern matching, clustering and evolution, tree construction, Hidden Markov Models, randomized algorithms.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 210, and 211; or COMP 401, and 410; and MATH 231, or 241; or BIOL 452; or MATH 553; or BIOL 525; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Artificial Intelligence
courses.description: Introduction to techniques and applications of modern artificial intelligence. Combinatorial search, probabilistic models and reasoning, and applications to natural language understanding, robotics, and computer vision.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 211 and 301; or COMP 401 and 410; as well as MATH 231; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Introduction to Machine Learning
courses.description: Machine learning as applied to speech recognition, tracking, collaborative filtering, and recommendation systems. Classification, regression, support vector machines, hidden Markov models, principal component analysis, and deep learning. Honors version available.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 211 and 301; or COMP 401 and 410; as well as MATH 233, 347, and STOR 435 or STOR 535 or BIOS 650; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisites.

courses.title: Computational Photography
courses.description: The course provides a hands on introduction to techniques in computational photography--the process of digitally recording light and then performing computational manipulations on those measurements to produce an image or other representation. The course includes an introduction to relevant concepts in computer vision and computer graphics.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 301; or COMP 401 and 410; as well as MATH 347 or 577; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Introduction to Computer Graphics
courses.description: Hardware, software, and algorithms for computer graphics. Scan conversion, 2-D and 3-D transformations, object hierarchies. Hidden surface removal, clipping, shading, and antialiasing. Not for graduate computer science credit.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 301 and 311; or COMP 401, 410 and 411; as well as MATH 347 or MATH 577; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Mathematics for Image Computing
courses.description: Mathematics relevant to image processing and analysis using real image computing objectives and provided by computer implementations.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 116 or 210 or 401, and MATH 233; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisites.

courses.title: Introduction to Computer Vision
courses.description: Fundamentals of Computer Vision and overview of recent research problems in Computer Vision. This course attempts to answer the following questions: (a) How do we capture and process an image? (b) How do we develop machine perception that recognizes, detects, and segments objects? (c) How do we connect the 3D world to 2D images and reconstruct 3D from images? The course covers the mathematical fundamentals and modern algorithms of computer vision, and how they can be useful to improving human lives and society.
courses.requisites: Pre- or corequisites, COMP 211, COMP 301, and MATH 347; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisites.

courses.title: Introduction to Robotics
courses.description: Hands-on introduction to robotics with a focus on the computational aspects. Students will build and program mobile robots. Topics include kinematics, actuation, sensing, configuration spaces, control, and motion planning. Applications include industrial, mobile, personal, and medical robots. Honors version available.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 301 and 311; or COMP 401, 410, and 411; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Natural Language Processing
courses.description: Through this course, students will develop an understanding of the general field of Natural Language Processing with an emphasis on state-of-the-art solutions for classic NLP problems. Topics include: text representation and classification, parts-of-speech tagging, parsing, translation, and language modeling.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, COMP 301 and COMP 311; a grade of C or better is required in all prerequisite courses.

courses.title: Topics in Computer Science
courses.description: This course has variable content and may be taken multiple times for credit. Different sections may be taken in the same semester. Honors version available.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: Special Topics in Computer Science, FC-KNOWING
courses.description: This course has variable content and may be taken multiple times for credit. Different sections may be taken in the same semester.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: Information Visualization
courses.description: Data is everywhere. Charts, graphs, and other types of information visualizations help people to make sense of data. This course explores the design, development, and evaluation of these visualizations. By combining aspects of design, computer graphics, HCI, and data science, you will gain hands-on experience with creating visualizations, using exploratory tools, and architecting data narratives. Topics include interactive systems, user-centered design, graphical perception and cognition, data storytelling, and insight building. Throughout this course, you will work directly with stakeholders to analyze data from a variety of domains and applications.

courses.title: Visualization Design Methods
courses.description: Data visualization combines computational, design, and cognitive principles to help people explore, communicate, and analyze large datasets. Developing effective visualizations often requires working closely with interdisciplinary teams to authentically reflect the needs of a data problem. This course will provide a hands-on introduction to common design methods for creating visualizations in different domains and problem constraints. Students will work with a variety of datasets to generate visualization solutions leveraging various design methodologies and media. Topics will include data sketching and crafting, user-centered design, task-driven design, cognitively-driven design, quantitative and qualitative experimental methods, and workshop methods.

courses.title: Operating System Implementation
courses.description: Students will learn how to write OS kernel code in C and a small amount of assembly. Students will implement major components of the OS kernel, such as page tables, scheduling, and program loading.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, COMP 530; a grade of B+ or better is required; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.

courses.title: Networked and Distributed Systems
