courses.title: Professional Development and Career-Readiness: Fourth Year Seminar I
courses.description: Professional Development and Career-Readiness: Fourth Year Seminar is designed to build students' skills in critical literature appraisal, application of data into the real-world practice environment, and intentional approach to team-based work. In addition, the course will build students' skills and readiness for entry into the post-graduate work or training environment.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, Student pharmacists must successfully complete all required coursework, including Immersion Experiences and elective requirements in the first, second, and third professional years.

courses.title: Professional Development and Career-Readiness: Fourth Year Seminar II
courses.description: Professional Development and Career-Readiness: Fourth Year Seminar is designed to build students' skills in critical literature appraisal, application of data into the real-world practice environment, and intentional approach to team-based work. In addition, the course will build students' skills and readiness for entry into the post-graduate work or training environment.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, Student pharmacists must successfully complete all required coursework, including Immersion Experiences and elective requirements in the first, second, and third professional years.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Who Was Socrates?
courses.description: Socrates is the quintessential philosopher--a man for all seasons, a foundational figure of the West.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Reason and Religion at the Dawn of Modern Science
courses.description: Students will read some of the most important philosophical reflections of the 17th and 18th centuries.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Theories in Human Nature
courses.description: Students will explore a variety of issues that arise when human beings begin to reflect on our own natures and will be introduced to main theories that have been developed. Honors version available.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Thinking about Time
courses.description: What is time? Do the past and the future exist, or only the present? Is the "flow of time" an objective feature of reality?

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Paradoxes
courses.description: Paradoxes have been a driving force in philosophy since the fourth century BCE. They force us to rethink old ideas and conceptions.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Abortion
courses.description: A general philosophical discussion of the value of life, the evil in death, and the wrongness of killing.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Race and Affirmative Action
courses.description: The goal of the course is to get a mature and correct understanding of race, racism, and affirmative action.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: From Vengeance to Mercy: Dealing with Evil
courses.description: This course will explore the ethical dimensions of the responses to evil that we have developed over history. Revenge, retribution, reparation; hatred, resentment, forgiveness; punishment, pardon, mercy.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Proofs of the Existence of God
courses.description: We will examine efforts in the history of philosophy to prove that God exists or that God does not exist. Our aim is to articulate and understand some of the underlying philosophical issues that are raised by these proofs and arguments. Honors version available.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Plato's Symposium and Its Influence on Western Art and Literature
courses.description: This seminar examines Plato's philosophical and literary masterpiece, The Symposium, and its influence on later artists and writers: we explore the Symposium itself, the ways in which the Symposium influenced later European artists and writers, and the importance of the Platonic view of love and beauty for modern artists and writers. Honors version available.

courses.title: First Year Seminar: The Self: Aspiration and Transformation
courses.description: Novels, memoirs, and aisles of self-help books attest to our desire to transform ourselves. Yet, the idea of self-transformation is puzzling. In this class, we will critically examine the idea of aspiration and transformation.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Philosophy with Children
courses.description: This seminar is designed to give students a unique, experiential perspective on philosophical inquiry by combining the philosophical study of ethics with virtual service in the community. We will examine philosophical questions about childhood and engage in philosophical interactions with children about a range of philosophical topics, with an emphasis on ethics and human values. Students perform 30 hours of service at a local K-5 school.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Mind, Brain, and Consciousness
courses.description: What are minds and how are they related to bodies?

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Philosophy through Mathematics
courses.description: This seminar introduces several of the central problems in philosophy through reflection on the nature of mathematics.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Ethics: Theoretical and Practical
courses.description: This seminar examines theoretical issues, relativism, utilitarianism, deontological ethics, and virtue ethics.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Issues in a World Society: Sports and Competition
courses.description: This seminar examines ethical issues in sports, including Title IX, gender equity, racism, sexism, cheating, violence, and drug use.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Moral Life
courses.description: This course will explore the meaning of basic moral concepts as they are understood in philosophy, science, and art. Honors version available.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Gateway to Philosophy, Politics, and Economics
courses.description: This course uses insights and techniques from philosophy, politics, and economics to answer questions like: What makes a modern civilization possible? How can our societies continue to improve? What role do property rights, markets, and political action play in creating flourishing civilizations? How do we address environmental degradation, distributive justice, and economic exploitation? Our answers will draw from rational choice theory, utility theory, game theory, public choice economics, etc. Course is limited to PPE minors.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Evil
courses.description: What is evil? Who, if anyone, is responsible for it? How different are evil people from the rest of us? How should we respond to them? The course will explore the nature of evil through philosophy, nonfiction, fiction, and film.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Is Free Will an Illusion?
courses.description: This course will examine whether our belief in freedom of action is compatible with the modern picture of ourselves. Honors version available.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Moral Weakness and Conscience
courses.description: Is man's reason a powerful thing: if one had knowledge or belief about something that should be done, would that be enough to position one to do it?

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Death as a Problem for Philosophy: Metaphysical and Ethical
courses.description: This course explores both old and new questions regarding death. It will examine the presuppositions and cogency of the classical religious-philosophical conception of death.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Words That Bind: The Structure of Constitutions
courses.description: In this seminar we will examine a number of constitutions and try to determine what makes a constitution better or worse, and when it makes sense to borrow constitutional principles from other countries. We will also try our hand at designing a constitution.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Short Stories and Contemporary Social Problems
courses.description: We will read short stories and social science articles that address social problems such as child-rearing; social mobility; mass incarceration and race; the opiate crisis; tradition versus science. Students will explore the different ways in which literature, the humanities and the social sciences construct issues of social relevance, the opportunities and limits of these constructions, and what might be gained by using each to understand and respond to these issues.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Reason, Religion, and Reality in the Copernican Revolution
courses.description: The arguments by which Galileo and his contemporaries defended the Copernican model of the solar system puzzle philosophers even today. Honors version available.

courses.title: First-Year Seminar: Persons and Identity
courses.description: An introduction to the topic of personal identity, focused on epistemological, ethical, and metaphysical themes. The course examines what personal identity over time consists in, whether and how we can know such identity, under what conditions our personal identity is liable to change, and what this implies for our values and projects.

courses.title: First Year Seminar: Special Topics
courses.description: Special Topics Course. Content will vary each semester.

courses.title: Introduction to Philosophy: Central Problems, Great Minds, Big Ideas
courses.description: An introduction to philosophy focusing on a few central problems, for example: free will, the basis of morality, the nature and limits of knowledge, and the existence of God. Honors version available.

courses.title: Introduction to Philosophy: Central Problems, Great Minds, Big Ideas
courses.description: This course introduces students to the experience of thinking like philosophers and aims at developing students' capacity to think carefully and critically about philosophical arguments. The central skills to be practiced are those involved in productive philosophical discussion. The course emphasizes how philosophy is and has been done through dialogue, that philosophical claims must be tested against the objections of one's fellow thinkers, and how philosophical disagreement can lead to productive insights.

courses.title: How to Reason and Argue: An Introduction to Critical Thinking
courses.description: A course on how to identify, analyze, and evaluate arguments by other people and how to construct arguments. Topics include argument reconstruction, informal logic, fallacies, introductory formal logic, probabilistic reasoning.

courses.title: Philosophical Texts that Changed the World: An Introduction to Philosophy through Great Works
courses.description: An introduction to philosophy focusing on several great books from the history of Western philosophy. See course description at the department's website for which books will be covered each semester. Students may not receive credit for both PHIL 110 and PHIL 113. Honors version available.

courses.title: Philosopher Queens: World Philosophies through Women's Texts
courses.description: This course provides an introduction to world philosophies through close readings of philosophical texts attributed to or written by women in different time-periods from across the globe. We will practice the art of reading, understanding, and philosophically engaging with great historical works of philosophy while also examining the political inequalities, social structures, and contemporary practices from within which these women philosophers wrote and were trying to make their voices heard.

courses.title: Making Sense of Ourselves
courses.description: An examination of some of the most influential attempts to understand human beings, their lives, and their moral and political values. Authors may include Plato, Aristotle, and Nietzsche. Honors version available.

courses.title: Philosophical Texts that Changed the World: An Introduction To Philosophy Through Great Works
courses.description: An introduction to philosophy focusing on several great books from the history of Western philosophy. See course description at the department's website for which books will be covered each semester. Special emphasis on practicing, engaging in, and discussing the activity of oral communication and communal deliberation. Students may not receive credit for both PHIL 113 and PHIL 110.

courses.title: Reason, Faith, and God: Philosophy of Western Religion
courses.description: A philosophical inquiry into the problems of religious experience and belief, as expressed in philosophic, religious, and literary documents from traditional and contemporary sources. Honors version available.

courses.title: Knowledge and Society
courses.description: An examination of questions about knowledge, evidence, and rational belief as they arise in areas of social life such as democratic politics, the law, science, religion, and education. Honors version available.

courses.title: AI and the Future of Humanity: Philosophical Issues about Technology and Human Survival
courses.description: This course investigates philosophical issues arising from advanced forms of technology, in particular artificial intelligence, virtual reality, and biological augmentation. We will consider questions about the dangers and benefits of AI, survival in non-biological ways, moral constraints on AI, the relationship between human and machine morality, and others. Honors version available.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Ethics of Emerging Technology
courses.description: Technology is reshaping our experiences in ways that, until recently, seemed like something out of science fiction: we now live in a world with generative AI assistants, self-driving cars, biometric authenticators, deepfakes, and DNA tests. How should we evaluate the impact these technologies have had and will have on our lives? In this course, we will apply methods of philosophical inquiry to carefully think through some of the moral questions raised by new technologies and provide a more nuanced evaluation of its impact on human activity.

courses.title: Language, Communication, and Human and Animal Minds
courses.description: An examination of the differences between natural human languages and other communication systems. Includes a philosophical inquiry into how languages relate to the world and the mind. Honors version available.

courses.title: Theory, Evidence, and Understanding in Science
courses.description: What is distinctive about the kind of knowledge called "science"? What is scientific explanation? How are scientific theories related to empirical evidence? Students may not receive credit for both PHIL 150 and PHIL 151. Honors version available.

courses.title: Theory, Evidence, and Understanding in Science (CommBeyond)
courses.description: What is distinctive about the kind of knowledge called ''science''? What is scientific explanation? How are scientific theories related to empirical evidence? An examination of these and related issues with special focus on developing oral communication skills. Students may not receive credit for both PHIL 151 and PHIL 150.

courses.title: Philosophy of the Social Sciences
courses.description: How do social sciences explain human actions? Are there social facts over and above facts about various individuals? Do values enter into social science?
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Truth and Proof: Introduction to Mathematical Logic
courses.description: Introduces the theory of deductive reasoning, using a symbolic language to represent and evaluate patterns of reasoning. Covers sentential logic and first-order predicate logic. Honors version available.

courses.title: Logic and Decision Theory
courses.description: A broader discussion of practical reasoning, including inductive and deductive logic, which provides a good introduction to decision and game theory that is important for the social sciences, especially economics. Honors version available.

courses.title: Virtue, Value, and Happiness: An Introduction to Moral Theory
courses.description: Exploration of different philosophical perspectives about right and wrong, personal character, justice, moral reasoning, and moral conflicts. Readings drawn from classic or contemporary sources. Critical discussion emphasized. Students may not receive credit for both PHIL 160 and PHIL 161. Honors version available.

courses.title: Virtue, Value, and Happiness: An Introduction to Moral Theory
courses.description: Exploration of different philosophical perspectives about right and wrong, personal character, justice, moral reasoning, and moral conflicts. Readings drawn from classic or contemporary sources. Special emphasis on practicing, engaging in, and discussing the activity of oral communication and communal deliberation. Students may not receive credit for both PHIL 160 and PHIL 161.

courses.title: Practical Ethics: Moral Reasoning and How We Live
courses.description: Topics may include war, medical ethics, media ethics, sexual ethics, business ethics, racism, sexism, capital punishment, and the environment. Honors version available.

courses.title: Morality and Business
courses.description: An examination of business ethics and the types of ethical dilemmas people may face in business practices.

courses.title: Bioethics
courses.description: An examination of ethical issues in the life sciences and technologies, medicine, public health, and/or human interaction with nonhuman animals or the living environment. Honors version available.

courses.title: Liberty, Rights, and Responsibilities: Introduction to Social Ethics and Political Thought
courses.description: An examination of major issues in political philosophy, e.g., liberty, individual rights, social responsibility, legal authority, civil authority, civil disobedience. Readings include classical and contemporary writings. Honors version available.

courses.title: Free Speech and the Norms of Public Discourse
courses.description: An investigation of the nature, value, and limits of free speech and viewpoint diversity, and of the norms we should adhere to when engaging in political discourse with one another. Uses the tools and methods of philosophical thought. Special attention to these questions in the setting of a contemporary university.

courses.title: Philosophical Foundations of American Democracy
courses.description: This course explores the political philosophies that shaped the United States, such as the Enlightenment, classical republicanism (liberty, self-government, rule of law), and constitutionalism. By reading and discussing a variety of philosophical and historical texts, students will learn how these ideas formed the foundation of American democracy and how later generations continued the effort to form "a more perfect union".

courses.title: Philosophy of Humor
courses.description: A course on philosophical issues related to laughter and humor. Historical and contemporary philosophical theories of humor; connections between traditional issues in aesthetics and humor; moral questions about humor, such as what is involved in a joke being racist/sexist/homophobic; and connections between jokes and various epistemological fallacies.

courses.title: Aesthetics and the Philosophy of Art
courses.description: The nature of art and artworks and their aesthetic appraisal. Honors version available.

courses.title: Special Topics in Philosophy, FC-VALUES
courses.description: Intensive exploration and discussion of selected topics in philosophy.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 9 total credits. 3 total completions.

courses.title: Wonder, Myth, and Reason: Introduction to Ancient Greek Science and Philosophy
courses.description: The emergence of philosophy in Greece during the sixth century BCE and its development during the classical period. The major figures studied are the Pre-Socratic philosophers, Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle. Honors version available.

courses.title: Perspectives on Gender, Race, and Marginality in Ancient Greek Philosophy, Science, and Medicine
courses.description: This course studies through the examination of several infamous, ignored, or otherwise uncharted Ancient Greek texts the views about gender and race as presented in ancient Greek philosophy, medicine, and science. Our aims are to generate a new understanding of how the male elite used such views to further promote or justify (or perhaps challenge) the existing marginalization and silencing of women, foreigners, and less privileged men.

courses.title: Asian Philosophy
courses.description: An examination of some of the philosophical traditions of Asia. Possible topics include Advaita Vedanta, Nyaya-Vaisheshika, Madhyamaka Buddhism, neo-Confucianism, Mohism, and philosophical Taoism.

courses.title: Medieval Philosophy
courses.description: A survey of medieval philosophy from Augustine through Ockham. Topics: God and the world, faith and reason, knowledge and reality, the problem of universals. Additional main authors: Anselm, Aquinas, Duns Scotus.

courses.title: 17th and 18th Century Western Philosophy
courses.description: A study of some major philosophical works from this period, including works by authors such as Descartes, Spinoza, Locke, Berkeley, Leibniz, Hume, and/or Kant. Honors version available.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Existential Philosophy and the Meaning(lessness) of Life
courses.description: A survey of European philosophers in the phenomenological and existentialist traditions. Philosophers studied may include Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Husserl, Heidegger, Sartre, Camus. Honors version available.

courses.title: American Philosophy
courses.description: An exploration of the distinctively American approaches to philosophy from Jonathan Edwards to the present.

courses.title: 20th-Century Western Philosophy
courses.description: An introductory survey of British and Continental philosophy in the 20th century.

courses.title: Mind, Matter, and Metaphysics: the Philosophy of Experience and Reality
courses.description: Topics in metaphysics and/or epistemology, such as: Is your mind different from your brain? Is it possible for us to know anything about the external world? Do we have free will? What distinguishes reasonable from unreasonable belief? Honors version available.

courses.title: Inductive Logic and the Scientific Method
courses.description: This course examines the role that inductive logic plays in scientific reasoning. Questions to be considered include: Are scientific theories distinguished from pseudoscience by being testable against our observations? Can we prove our best scientific theories to be true? Are we justified in making predictions about the future on the basis of past observations? The course examines these and other questions about confirming scientific theories by using the apparatus provided by the probability calculus.

courses.title: Ethics in Action
courses.description: Ethics Bowl provides a unique experiential opportunity for students to apply theory to practical global issues. Students will prepare cases to present locally and at Ethics Bowl competition. Permission of the instructor.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: Ethics, Politics, and Technology
courses.description: In the near future, our taxis will be driver-less, our wars will be fought by autonomous drones, and our towns will be kept safe by algorithms foreseeing crimes. This course explores the ethical implications of this new technological revolution and invites students to debate the challenges it engenders. We will debate how new technologies ought to be governed and what limits should be imposed on their implementation.

courses.title: Not All Fun and Games: Ethics of Sports
courses.description: An analysis of the moral significance of sports, the nature of sport and competition, and issues such as racism, gender equity, violence, and performance-enhancing drugs.

courses.title: The Ethics of Peace, War, and Defense
courses.description: An analysis of ethical issues that arise in peace, war, and defense, e.g., the legitimacy of states, just war theory, terrorism, weapons of mass destruction.

courses.title: Justice, Rights, and the Common Good: Philosophical Perspectives on Social and Economic Issues
courses.description: This course will focus on justice and the common good, applying theoretical justifications to contemporary social and economic issues. Readings will include classical and contemporary literature on the nature of justice and rights. Honors version available.

courses.title: Race, Racism, and Social Justice: African-American Political Philosophy
courses.description: Race, identity, discrimination, multiculturalism, affirmative action, and slave reparations in the writings of Walker, Delany, Douglass, Cooper, DuBois, King, and Malcolm X. Honors version available.

courses.title: Moral and Philosophical Issues of Gender in Society
courses.description: A survey of feminist perspectives on topics such as the meaning of oppression, sexism and racism, sex roles and stereotypes, ideals of female beauty, women in the workplace, pornography, rape. Honors version available.

courses.title: Ideology, Capitalism, and Critique
courses.description: This course studies how (oftentimes implicit) ideological commitments shape our culture and our social reality. We will explore the Marxist tradition and the Frankfurt School Critical Theory, as well as contemporary applications and critiques of ideology in thinkers such as Jaeggi, Fraser, Shelby, and Haslanger.

courses.title: Latin American Philosophy
courses.description: This class addresses perennial philosophical questions about existence, morality, knowledge, and meaning through texts and authors from Latin America. The clash of conquistadors with pre-Columbian peoples, the wars of independence, and the unique mestizo heritage of Latin America provide a rich context to frame traditional philosophical questions in a new light.

courses.title: Morality, Law, and Justice: Issues in Legal Philosophy
courses.description: Explores issues in legal philosophy such as, What is law? Does it serve justice or undermine it? Can punishment be justified? When is a person responsible? Honors version available.

courses.title: Human Rights: Philosophical Interrogations
courses.description: The philosophy of human rights addresses questions about the existence, content, nature, universality, justification, and legal status of human rights. The strong claims made on behalf of human rights frequently provoke skeptical doubts and countering philosophical defenses. These will be addressed through classical and contemporary history of philosophy.

courses.title: Moral and Philosophical Issues in Education
courses.description: A critical examination of the moral and philosophical issues in education: What does it mean to be well educated? What is a liberal education? Honors version available.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Field Work in Philosophy: Introducing Philosophy in Primary and Secondary Schools
courses.description: Permission of the instructor. This course combines on-campus structured learning with substantial on-site field work incorporating philosophy into the primary and/or secondary school curriculum. Philosophy subjects and school partners will vary by semester.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 9 total credits. 3 total completions.

courses.title: Philosophy across the Lifespan
courses.description: This is a high-impact service-learning course that aims to promote experiential learning in philosophy by combining traditional elements of classroom study with service in the community (HI-SERVICE). Students will have the unique opportunity to teach and learn philosophy alongside older adults in the Triangle area, thereby integrating the academic study of philosophy with community engagement.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, One prior Philosophy course required.

courses.title: Reasoning Together: Philosophy through Dialogue and Podcast
courses.description: What does it take to speak and listen philosophically? How do we think and inquire together? This course is a hands-on exploration of how to link out loud through an engagement with one of the most popular philosophical mediums: podcasts. Students will reflect on and engage in meaningful, rigorous, and respectful philosophical conversation, even when the topic is abstract, personal, or controversial.

courses.title: Special Topics in Philosophy, FC-KNOWING
courses.description: Intensive exploration and discussion of selected topics in philosophy.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 9 total credits. 3 total completions.

courses.title: Philosophy as a Way of Life: Spiritual Exercise across the Globe
courses.description: What does it mean to live philosophically? This course presents philosophy not only as an intellectual discipline, but also as a way of life and as a global, transformative practice. Students explore how classical and pre-modern traditions from around the world championed diverse forms of spiritual and ethical self-cultivation.

courses.title: Metaphysics
courses.description: An examination of general theories of the nature of reality. What kinds of things exist? What are space, time, and causation? Are abstract entities (such as numbers) real?

courses.title: Theory of Knowledge
courses.description: What is knowledge and how does it relate to belief, justification, and truth? What makes beliefs reasonable or irrational? Can skepticism be defeated?

courses.title: Philosophy of Mind
courses.description: The mind-body problem, the nature of thinking, the puzzles of consciousness, and the qualitative character of felt experience.

courses.title: Philosophy of Language
courses.description: Survey of major topics in contemporary philosophy of language. Topics may include truth and meaning, speech acts, reference, descriptions, names, and demonstratives.

courses.title: Philosophy of Physics
courses.description: Topics may include the nature of space and time, the ontological status of fields and energy, or causation and locality in quantum physics. Honors version available.

courses.title: Sex and Death, Life and Health, Species and Evolution: The Philosophy of Biology
courses.description: Philosophical issues raised by biological theories, which may include the logical structure of evolutionary theory, fitness, taxonomy, the notion of a living thing, reductionism, evolutionary explanations, or teleology.

courses.title: Minds and Machines: Philosophy of Cognitive Science
courses.description: Philosophical questions raised by linguistics, computer science, cognitive psychology, and neuroscience. Topics may include the innateness of language, artificial intelligence, and the neural correlates of consciousness. Honors version available.

courses.title: Quantum Mechanics, Weirdness, and Reality
courses.description: An interdisciplinary course on the weirdness of quantum mechanics and the problem of interpreting it. Nonlocality, the measurement problem, superpositions, Bohm's theory, collapse theories, and the many-worlds interpretation.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, MATH 231 and any PHYS course numbered 100 or greater; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisites.

courses.title: Intermediate Mathematical Logic
courses.description: Quantificational logic with identity; basic meta-theory; modal logic.

courses.title: Induction, Probability, and Confirmation
courses.description: Current accounts of evidence and observation, the confirmation of scientific theories, the logic of inductive reasoning, and the metaphysics and epistemology of chance.

courses.title: Major Developments in Ethics: Historical and Philosophical Perspectives
courses.description: PHIL 160 recommended. Major developments in the history of moral philosophy, from Plato to Nietzsche. Honors version available.

courses.title: Contemporary Ethical Theory
courses.description: Using 20th- and 21st-century texts, this course explores some general questions about morality in depth. For example, Is there moral truth? Are any moral rules absolute? Why be moral? Honors version available.

courses.title: Ethics and Economics
courses.description: Recommended preparation, at least one course in ethics (PHIL 160, 163, or 170) or one course in economics. Issues at the intersection of ethics and economics, including value; the relation between values and preferences; rationality; the relevance to economics of rights, justice, and the value of human life.

courses.title: Living Things, Wilderness, and Ecosystems: An Introduction to Environmental Ethics
courses.description: The meaning of environmental values and their relation to other values; the ethical status of animals, species, wilderness, and ecosystems; the built environment; environmental justice; ecofeminism; obligations to future generations. Honors version available.

courses.title: Authority, Freedom, and Rights: Advanced Political Philosophy
courses.description: Advanced discussion of competing philosophical approaches to questions of justice, authority, freedom, rights, and the like, including libertarianism, liberalism, communitarianism, Marxism, and feminism.

courses.title: Philosophy and Film
courses.description: An examination of how philosophical issues are explored in the medium of film. Honors version available.

courses.title: Gateway to Philosophy, Politics, and Economics
courses.description: One course in economics strongly recommended. This interdisciplinary gateway course provides an introduction to subjects and quantitative techniques used to analyze problems in philosophy, political science, and economics. Honors version available.

courses.title: Seminar in Selected Topics
courses.description: Intensive exploration and discussion of selected topics in philosophy. Honors version available.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 9 total credits. 3 total completions.

courses.title: Ethics Research Seminar for Undergraduates
courses.description: This is a capstone course in ethics designed for Parr Center Ethics Scholars completing the Mentored Research capstone project. The seminar will provide a collaborative learning space that will facilitate each student's independent research and writing. This course will begin with survey of major themes in practical ethics before transitioning to a thematically focused study of topics based on the research interests of the students in the course.

courses.title: Undergraduate Research Seminar in Selected Topics
courses.description: This is a philosophical research course for anyone with some background in philosophy and an interest in the topic. Special emphasis is placed on giving students the opportunity to immerse themselves in a research project that leads to an original final research paper.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Directed Readings
courses.description: Permission of the instructor. See the director of undergraduate studies of the department.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 9 total credits. 3 total completions.

courses.title: Philosophy Research Seminar for Undergraduates
courses.description: This course is designed to approximate the experience of a graduate seminar in philosophy. The course topic is different each year; class meetings are discussion-based and focused on developing professional writing and research skills. Recommended for all majors and minors.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 9 total credits. 3 total completions.

courses.title: Aristotle
courses.description: An examination of some representative works of Aristotle, with reference to common emphases and basic problems, together with an analysis of their philosophic content. The aim to provide students with a more thorough understanding of the key texts, doctrines, notions, and ideas in Aristotle's philosophy as a whole and with the capacities and confidence to conduct a short, independent, ancient philosophical research project on Aristotle's philosophy.

courses.title: Plato
courses.description: An examination of some representative works in the context of contemporary scholarship.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Ancient Greco-Roman Medicine and Philosophy
courses.description: This cross-listed course offers a high-level coverage of central texts in Ancient Greco-Roman Medicine with the aim of providing students with a thorough understanding of the philosophical foundations of Western medicine.

courses.title: Medieval Philosophy
courses.description: An intensive study of some medieval philosophical author (e.g., Aquinas, Scotus, or Ockham) or topic (e.g., arguments for the existence of God, universals, knowledge of individuals).
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Rationalism
courses.description: An in-depth study of such rationalist philosophers as Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Empiricism
courses.description: An in-depth study of such empiricist philosophers as Locke, Berkeley, and Hume.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Kant's Theoretical Philosophy
courses.description: An intensive introduction to Kant's accounts of space, time, concepts, perception, substance, causation, and the thinking self through a careful study of his masterwork, The Critique of Pure Reason.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Kant's Practical Philosophy
courses.description: This course studies closely Kant's practical philosophy, dedicated to understanding and assessing the answers that Kant gives to classic questions of practical philosophy, such as: What does morality demand from us? What is the morally right course of action? Is morality objective? Do moral norms depend on God?
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Nietzsche
courses.description: This course examines the philosophy of Friedrich Nietzsche, covering all three conventionally recognized periods of his philosophy in chronological sequence, tracing the historical and philosophical development of his views from the early Birth of Tragedy to the late Twilight of Idols. The main question we will face when studying all these different writings is how Nietzsche tries to solve the problem of nihilism. Completion of one previous PHIL course preferred.

courses.title: Hegel
courses.description: In-depth study of Hegel's systematic philosophy emphasizing its roots in Kant's critical philosophy. Primary focus on Phenomenology of Spirit, supplemented by selections from the Encyclopedia and Philosophy of Right.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: History of American Philosophy
courses.description: An in-depth study of American contributions to philosophy, including for example the transcendentalists, the pragmatists, Quine, Rorty, and others.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: The Beginnings of Analytic Philosophy
courses.description: Frege, Russell, Moore, and Wittgenstein among others are considered.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, PHIL 155 and two additional philosophy courses are recommended as background.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Current Issues in Analytic Philosophy
courses.description: Two courses in philosophy other than PHIL 155 strongly recommended. Recent work in epistemology and metaphysics.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 9 total credits. 3 total completions.

courses.title: Philosophy of Mind
courses.description: At least two courses in philosophy other than PHIL 155, including PHIL 340, strongly recommended. An examination of dualism, behaviorism, the identity theory, and forms of functionalism with special focus on the problems of mental aboutness and the problems of consciousness.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Philosophical Foundations of Artificial Intelligence
courses.description: This course focuses on advanced philosophical issues tied to artificial intelligence. We will discuss a number of topics concerning how to understand contemporary AI systems, their limits and advantages, as well as the risks and benefits of their application and deployment in real life situations. PHIL 143 or a course on machine learning is strongly recommended but not required.

courses.title: Advanced Philosophy of Language
courses.description: At least two courses in philosophy other than PHIL 155, including PHIL 345, strongly recommended. A study of important contemporary contributions in philosophy of language. Topics include meaning, reference, and truth.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Philosophy of Natural Sciences
courses.description: An in-depth survey of general issues in contemporary philosophy of natural science intended for advanced philosophy students. Topics include confirmation, explanation, theory-choice, realism, reduction.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Philosophy of Physics
courses.description: Topics may include the nature of space and time, the ontological status of fields and energy, or causation and locality in quantum physics.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Philosophy of Biology
courses.description: The logical structure of evolutionary theory, fitness, taxonomy, the notion of a living thing, reductionism, evolutionary explanations, teleology.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Philosophy of Psychology
courses.description: Topics may include reasoning, the relationship between language and thought, concepts, moral cognition, and emotions.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Philosophy, History, and the Social Sciences
courses.description: The nature of historical explanation, structural and functional explanation, the weighing of historical testimony, the concept of meaning, normative judgments and predictions in the social sciences.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Symbolic Logic
courses.description: Introduction for graduates and advanced undergraduates.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, PHIL 155; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Advanced Symbolic Logic
courses.description: Presupposes propositional and quantificational logic as a basis of further deductive development with special attention to selected topics: alternative systems, modal and deontic logic, inductive logic, the grammar of formalized languages, paradoxes, and foundations of mathematics.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 12 total credits. 4 total completions.

courses.title: Set Theory and Logic
courses.description: Natural and real numbers. Infinite cardinal and ordinal numbers. Alternative axiom systems and their consistency problems.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, PHIL 455; permission of the instructor for students lacking the prerequisite.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Formal Techniques in Philosophy
courses.description: In a variety of subfields of philosophy, philosophers have found formal techniques to be useful tools for making progress on important philosophical questions. These subfields include, but are not limited to: metaphysics, epistemology, philosophy of language, philosophy of mind, ethics, and political philosophy. This course is a general introduction to some of the formal tools that have been most influential in these fields.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, For undergraduates: PHIL 155 or equivalent, or permission of the instructor.

courses.title: Philosophy of Mathematics
courses.description: Philosophical problems concerning logic and the foundation of mathematics.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: History of Moral Philosophy
courses.description: Examination of classic texts of Plato, Aristotle, Aquinas, Hobbes, Butler, Hume, Kant, and Mill. Selections may vary from year to year.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, Two courses in philosophy other than PHIL 155, including PHIL 360, strongly recommended.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Contemporary Moral Philosophy
courses.description: Advanced discussion of moral issues such as fact and value, reason and morality, the nature of morality.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, two courses in philosophy, including one in value theory.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 9 total credits. 3 total completions.

courses.title: Contemporary Moral and Social Problems
courses.description: Two courses in philosophy other than PHIL 155 strongly recommended. A detailed examination of one or more of the following contemporary issues: environmental ethics, animal rights, abortion, euthanasia, pornography, racism, sexism, public versus private morality.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Moral Responsibility
courses.description: An intensive study of classic and recent work on the nature of moral responsibility and its relationship to blame (and praise).
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, one previous course in philosophy, preferably in value theory.

courses.title: Justice in Health Care
courses.description: One course in philosophy strongly recommended. Medical students welcome. The course will focus on the question of how scarce health care resources ought to be distributed in order to meet the demands of justice.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Risk and Society
courses.description: One additional course in philosophy strongly recommended. The course examines attitudes toward risk and how they affect our preferences for different public policies in the areas of environmental protection, technology regulation, and workplace and product safety.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Political Philosophy from Hobbes to Rousseau
courses.description: Two courses in philosophy other than PHIL 155, including PHIL 170 or 370, strongly recommended. Explores the foundations of justice and authority in the idea of contract or covenant, the nature of law, rights, liberty, and democracy in the work of Hobbes, Locke, Hume, Rousseau.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Topics in 19th Century Philosophy
courses.description: An examination of central issues in social and political philosophy as they figure in the work of 19th Century Philosophy.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: American Political Philosophy
courses.description: One course in philosophy other than PHIL 155 strongly recommended. The issue of unity and diversity in America is analyzed through the writings of Jefferson, the Federalists and Anti-Federalists, Calhoun, MacKinnon, DuBois, and Rawls.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Foundations of Modern Political Philosophy
courses.description: This course traces the emergence and development of central themes of modern political philosophy from the 13th through the 17th century.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Philosophical Issues in Gender, Race, and Class
courses.description: Examines in greater depth and complexity one or more of the issues addressed in PHIL 275, investigating issues of gender, race, and class within the dominant theories of philosophy.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Recent Developments in Political Philosophy
courses.description: Two courses in philosophy other than PHIL 155, including PHIL 370, strongly recommended. Investigation of major contemporary contributors (Rawls, Nozick, Dworkin, Cohen, Waldron, Arrow) to philosophical debate concerning justice, equality, liberty, democracy, public reason, or rights versus community.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 9 total credits. 3 total completions.

courses.title: Philosophy of Law
courses.description: An exploration of whether and under what conditions the state has the right to control crime by punishment of past crimes and preventive detention to prevent future crimes.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Philosophy and Literature
courses.description: Philosophical readings of literary texts, including novels, plays, and poems.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Philosophy of Art
courses.description: Competing theories of art and art criticism. The relationship between art and emotional expression, the formal character of art, and standards of taste.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Health Care, Science, and Philosophy
courses.description: Interdisciplinary course to develop critical thinking capacities through philosophical study of the nature of scientific presuppositions and concepts, including events, causality, and determinism, with specific application to health care issues.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Existentialism and Phenomenology
courses.description: A study of one or two major systematic works by Sartre, Heidegger, or Merleau-Ponty.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Advanced Directed Studies
courses.description: Permission of the director of undergraduate studies. Advanced independent work in philosophy.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 9 total credits. 3 total completions.

courses.title: Ethics, Responsibility, and Justice
courses.description: Ethics explores obligations to act in the interest of others as well as ourselves. Justice explores the ways people should organize and govern themselves. Course addresses such questions as, What principles govern our relationships with other people? What do we owe others and ourselves? How should we treat other people?
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 2 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Philosophy, Politics, and Economics: Capstone Course
courses.description: Permission of the department. The Capstone Seminar is the final course in the PPE sequence. The seminar has two components: a set of readings that focus on cutting edge work at the intersection of Philosophy, Political Science, and Economics and individual research projects selected in consultation with the instructor. The project involves giving a presentation to, and getting feedback from, seminar participants, and culminates in a final research paper. Throughout, participants will be actively engaging with each other, deepening their understanding of core concepts and tools of PPE, and applying them to specific issues.

courses.title: Principles of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences
courses.description: This course introduces the profession of pharmacy and the pharmaceutical sciences. An examination of the fundamental principles underlying both fields promotes an understanding that includes historical developments, issues and controversies, contemporary challenges and opportunities for innovation, and career opportunities. Importantly, students explore strategies for pharmaceutical research and care in the contexts of FDA-regulated drug development and the roles of pharmaceuticals in healthcare.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, CHEM 261; Pre- or corequisites, CHEM 262 and MATH 231.

courses.title: Research in Pharmaceutical Sciences
courses.description: Permission must be granted by the course instructor prior to enrollment. This course is a supervised experiential research experience in a pharmaceutical sciences laboratory. Students engage in a mentored, in-depth, scholarly project wherein they frame an answerable question with a faculty course instructor, generate and interpret relevant data, and communicate their findings in written form.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Innovations and Transformations in Pharmaceutical Sciences
courses.description: Students will learn about and develop skills in topics related to the drug development pipeline (from discover, delivery, clinical pharmacology, and outcomes), pharmacy practice, and professional development. Programming consists of classroom sessions, guest speakers, panels, simulations, and site visits to hospitals, community pharmacies, and different pharmaceutical industries. Classroom sessions will be led by graduate students, post-doctoral fellows, and faculty. The classroom experience will be active learning to immerse students in scientific discourse. Restricted to learners participating in the UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy ITPS Program.

courses.title: Fundamentals of Regulatory Affairs
courses.description: This foundational pharmaceutical science course will provide an overview of regulatory affairs with a focus on global pharmaceutical product development. Students will learn about medical product regulation in the United States and key international markets. Students will also learn about the process for obtaining and maintaining marketing approval along with tools and approaches used by regulatory professionals. This didactic course will be taught asynchronously but will include regular touch points.

courses.title: Making Medicines: Drug Discovery, Development, and Approval
courses.description: This course introduces the pharmaceutical sciences as a scientific discipline by facilitating student exploration of how new drugs are developed from the initial concept to the patient. Students gain an understanding of each stage through self-paced, asynchronous interaction with online videos highlighting the fundamental processes and rigor drug manufacturers undertake to research, develop, and deliver new medicines to patients. In class, students will engage in case-based discussions with experienced drug development professionals.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, CHEM 261; Corequisites, CHEM 261L, CHEM 262 and MATH 231.

courses.title: Biochemical Foundations of Chemical Biology
courses.description: This course covers core biochemical and molecular biology techniques, concepts, and tools used to conduct research at the interface of chemistry and biology. Topics include enzymology, characterization of drug-target interactions, mechanisms-based inhibitor design, assay design and development, targeting kinases and GPCRs, biopharmaceuticals, gene therapy, nucleic-acid binding agents, information-based drugs, chemical tools to study epigenetics, harnessing biosynthetic pathways for chemical diversity, and other recent advances and techniques in drug discovery.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, BIOC 107 and CHEM 262 or 262H, or CHEM 430, or CHEM 431, or CHEM 432.

courses.title: Molecular Foundations of Chemical Biology: Organic and Medicinal Chemistry
courses.description: Organic chemistry, broadly writ (i.e., not just synthesis), underlies nearly every endeavor in medicinal chemistry (the search for new drugs) and chemical biology (the use of chemical tools to understand biology). This course provides a review of important concepts in organic chemistry as they apply to biological research. Topics include a review of intermolecular interactions as they apply to biological structures and function, a discussion of how small molecules interact with their targets.

courses.title: Evaluation Research and Project Design
courses.description: This course will include formal instruction on evaluation research, study design, and data analyses that would be encountered in a health system pharmacy administration workplace. This course is designed to provide a broad survey of critical evaluation components, and students are encouraged to explore any topic in more depth, as needed or desired.

courses.title: Foundations in Implementation Science: Examples in Precision Health and Society
courses.description: This course will cover the fundamentals of implementation science using examples in precision health (e.g., targeted therapies, pharmacogenomics, and tailored treatment plans). More specifically, we will discuss frameworks, strategies, study designs, and outcomes related to implementation science using examples related to the implementation of precision health in research and practice. We will apply these learnings to implementation challenges, so that future pharmacists and researchers alike can consider the application.
courses.requisites: Prerequisites, SOCI 172 and SPHG 101, or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Data Science in Pharmacy
courses.description: This data science elective course is intended to provide students with baseline knowledge of core competencies in data science and its applications across the health sciences landscape and prepares students to become successful in their profession. Pharmacists will encounter data science in different contexts throughout their careers. ASHP describes such ''informatics'' projects as including creation of clinical decision support; ensuring accuracy of medication order intent; and guiding clinicians to appropriate medication use.

courses.title: Drug Delivery and Nanomedicine I
courses.description: This course covers fundamental concepts in drug delivery systems and nanomedicine, including the preparation of journal articles, drug carriers, molecular forces, thermodynamics, and various drug transport mechanisms. It also delves into advanced topics such as in vitro and in vivo models, experimental design, and the pharmacokinetics of nanomedicines, providing a comprehensive understanding of the field.

courses.title: Drug Delivery and Nanomedicine II
courses.description: Students will explore polymer science fundamentals, including molecular weights (Mn, Mw), polydispersity index (PDI), and stimuli-responsive polymers. The curriculum covers step-growth and chain-growth reactions, polymerization methods (ATRP, RAFT), the regular solution model, LCST, UCST, theta temperature, and the Flory-Huggins model. Additionally, students will learn about polyelectrolytes, suspensions, emulsions, PEGylation, click chemistry, and nanoparticles in drug delivery. Additionally, the course will explore theranostics, microfabrication techniques, and the latest advancements in drug delivery systems for delivery to various regions of the body. Also, wearable sensors and diagnostics for low-income settings will be discussed.

courses.title: Pharmaceutical Sciences Seminar in Chemical Biology and Medicinal Chemistry
courses.description: This course, which offered in both the Fall and Spring semesters, provides a deep look at contemporary research in Chemical Biology and Medicinal Chemistry as a pharmaceutical sciences discipline. The class format consists of seminar presentations by experts in the field, including invited outside scientists, faculty members, or doctoral candidates. Students are expected to actively engage in seminar activities and participate in impromptu discussions.

courses.title: Pharmaceutical Sciences Seminar in Pharmacotherapy and Experimental Therapeutics
courses.description: This course, which offered in both the Fall and Spring semesters, provides a deep look at contemporary research in Pharmacotherapy and Experimental Therapeutics as a pharmaceutical sciences discipline. The class format consists of seminar presentations by experts in the field, including invited outside scientists, faculty members, or doctoral candidates. Students are expected to actively engage in seminar activities and participate in impromptu discussions.

courses.title: Pharmaceutical Sciences Seminar in Pharmacoengineering and Molecular Pharmaceutics
courses.description: This course, which offered in both the Fall and Spring semesters, provides a deep look at contemporary research in Pharmacoengineering and Molecular Pharmaceutics as a pharmaceutical sciences discipline. The class format consists of seminar presentations by experts in the field, including invited outside scientists, faculty members, or doctoral candidates. Students are expected to actively engage in seminar activities and participate in impromptu discussions.

courses.title: Pharmaceutical Sciences Seminar in Pharmaceutical Outcomes and Policy
courses.description: This course, which offered in both the Fall and Spring semesters, provides a deep look at contemporary research in Pharmaceutical Outcomes and Policy as a pharmaceutical sciences discipline. The class format consists of seminar presentations by experts in the field, including invited outside scientists, faculty members, or doctoral candidates. Students are expected to actively engage in seminar activities and participate in impromptu discussions.

courses.title: Making Medicines
courses.description: This foundational pharmaceutical science course will provide an overview of the pharmaceutical product development process including challenges and issues associated with each phase. Students will learn how pharmaceutical products are identified for development and key steps in obtaining and maintaining market approval. Students will also learn about business aspects that drive the development strategy. This graduate-level didactic course will be taught asynchronously.

courses.title: Fundamentals of Regulatory Affairs
courses.description: This foundational regulatory science course will provide an overview of regulatory affairs with a focus on global pharmaceutical product development. Students will learn about pharmaceutical product regulation in the US and other key international markets. Students will also learn about the process for obtaining and maintaining marketing approval along with tools and approaches used by regulatory professionals. This graduate-level didactic course will be taught asynchronously but will include regular touch points.

courses.title: Preclinical Development
courses.description: This foundational pharmaceutical science course will cover preclinical aspects of pharmaceutical product development and how they contribute to the regulatory approval process. Students will learn about the processes of drug discovery, lead optimization, and compound formulation, as well as in vitro and in vivo approaches to assess drug metabolism and pharmacokinetics, pharmacology, and toxicology. This graduate-level didactic course will be taught asynchronously but will include regular touch points with course instructors and other students.

courses.title: Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls
courses.description: This foundational pharmaceutical science course will provide an overview of chemistry, manufacturing, and controls in pharmaceutical product development and how they differ by product type. Students will learn about the processes of assay development, manufacturing, and quality control for small molecules, biologics, and gene and cell therapies. Students will also learn about regulatory submissions and inspections. This graduate-level didactic course will be taught asynchronously but will include regular touch points.

courses.title: Clinical Development
courses.description: This foundational pharmaceutical science course will cover clinical aspects of pharmaceutical product development and contributions to the regulatory process. Students will study the phases of clinical development and considerations for trial design, conduct, and evaluation of data. Students will also learn about bioethics and differences in clinical research in the US and key international markets. This graduate-level didactic course will be taught asynchronously but will include regular touch points with course instructors and other students.

courses.title: Postmarketing Topics
courses.description: This foundational pharmaceutical science course will cover postmarketing aspects of pharmaceutical product development and how they contribute to maintaining regulatory approval. Students will learn about activities that help to further evaluate and exploit the full potential of a marketed pharmaceutical product including supply chain, sales and marketing, pharmacovigilance, risk management, and postmarketing research. This graduate-level didactic course will be taught asynchronously but will include regular touch points with course instructors and other students.

courses.title: Biostatistics
courses.description: This foundational pharmaceutical science course will teach basic statistical concepts used frequently during pharmaceutical product development. Students will learn the statistical terminology and approaches that are used to initiate a research investigation, plan a clinical trial, and analyze data. Students will also learn about the role of the statistician in pharmaceutical product development. This graduate-level didactic course will be taught asynchronously but will include regular touch points with course instructors and other students.

courses.title: Emerging Topics in Regulatory Science
courses.description: This foundational pharmaceutical science course will provide an overview of regulatory science with focus on FDA regulatory science priorities related to innovation in pharmaceutical product development. Students will learn about current research aimed at modernizing toxicology, innovating clinical research and personalized medicine, improving manufacturing and quality, and strengthening social and behavioral science. This graduate-level didactic course will be taught asynchronously but will include regular touch points with course instructors and other students.

courses.title: Seminars in Chromatin and Epigenetics
courses.description: Designed to expose students to the broad epigenetic research interests of our large epigenetics focused faculty and expose students to a broad range of epigenetics research techniques.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 1 total credits. 2 total completions.

courses.title: Fundamentals of Therapeutic Market Analysis: A Molecules to Market Course
courses.description: Fundamentals of Therapeutic Market Analysis: A Molecules to Market Course is an 8-week, asynchronous, online course that provides an introduction to therapeutic market analysis, explaining epidemiological principles and methods and their applications in business situations. We will explore such topics as potential revenue line for drugs, drug payer channels and trends, and the role of qualitative and quantitative research. The course is divided into five modules. Each module includes 1-11 self-spaced sessions that should take 30-90 mins to complete.

courses.title: Translational Science: A Molecules to Market Course
courses.description: Translational Science: A Molecules to Market Course is an asynchronous, online course that will teach participants the key components of an effective research and development workplan for translating a drug-development idea to the market. A workplan is a subset of a business plan that describes the small molecule characteristics (including potency, stability, specificity, and other attributes) and the criteria of each that are required to justify advancing the small molecule for development. The course is divided into five modules. Each module includes 1-9 self-spaced sessions that should each take 30-90 mins to complete.

courses.title: Fundamentals of Global Regulatory Affairs
courses.description: This foundational pharmaceutical science course will provide an overview of regulatory affairs with a focus on global pharmaceutical product development. Students will learn about drug and biologics regulation in the US, EU, UK, Japan, and Australia. Students will also learn about the process for obtaining and maintaining global marketing approval along with tools and approaches used by regulatory professionals. This graduate-level didactic course will be taught asynchronously but will include regular touch points with course instructors and other students.

courses.title: Global Leadership in the Pharmaceutical Sciences
courses.description: This course aims to stimulate your thinking about pharmacy leadership within the pharmaceutical sciences and foster a sense of responsibility for your personal and professional development. The course will expose you to various principles and practices of leaders. It will also explore ethics as it pertains to leadership and business principles within the pharmaceutical industry and discuss different methods to handle employees within the workplace. The course is intended to challenge you to reflect on the complexities surrounding leadership and leading others, as well as your leadership motivation. Each class session, activity, and assessment require your preparation and thoughtful engagement.

courses.title: Emerging Topics in Global Regulatory Science
courses.description: This foundational pharmaceutical science course will focus on emerging topics in global regulatory science related to innovations in pharmaceutical product development and distribution. Students will learn about current research aimed at modernizing toxicology, innovating clinical research and personalized medicine, improving manufacturing and quality, and strengthening social and behavioral science. This graduate-level didactic course will be taught asynchronously but will include regular touch points with course instructors and other students.

courses.title: Financial and Data Management in Global Medicines Development
courses.description: This course prepares students to apply financial, analytical, and strategic principles across the full lifecycle of global medicines development. Students will build skills in financial modeling, Excel, and generative AI; design and measure data strategies; and develop comprehensive business cases and operating plans. Core topics include finance and accounting fundamentals, cost-effectiveness and ROI analysis, market access strategies, project management, venture capital, and pathways to product launch. Emphasis is placed on data visualization, storytelling, and ethical considerations in data collection and interpretation, enabling students to create and evaluate sustainable, evidence-based business plans in the global biopharmaceutical arena.

courses.title: Innovations and Transformations in Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences Advanced
courses.description: Students will take a an intensive look into a specific area within the lifespan of the drug (drug discovery, drug delivery, pharmacotherapy, clinical practice, or pharmaceutical outcomes). They will learn about background knowledge, recent research innovations, and practice specific skills related to this area. This course will offer programming consisting of lectures and hands-on application based activities. The classroom experience will be active learning as much as possible to immerse students in scientific discourse.

courses.title: Foundations for Cross-Disciplinary Training in the Pharmaceutical Sciences
courses.description: This is a required course for first year pharmaceutical sciences graduate students. Students participate on cross-discipline teams to discuss topics in three foundational areas essential to their development as pharmaceutical scientists: research ethics which meets RCR training requirements; leading research articles within five areas of pharmaceutical sciences; and professional development.

courses.title: Drug Development and Professional Skills Development
courses.description: Students will learn about and develop skills in topics related to pharmaceutical development and professional development. The Common Core is an interdisciplinary environment with students from each of the four Divisional PhD programs.
courses.requisites: Prerequisite, First year graduate student in Pharmaceutical Sciences or instructor permission required.

courses.title: Regulatory Communication
courses.description: This advanced pharmaceutical science course will train students on strategic elements to consider when preparing for communications with regulators necessary to support and maintain pharmaceutical product marketing approval and advise on regulatory agency interactions. Students will learn how clarity and brevity should drive both presenting and summarizing of science and data considering the regulations. This graduate-level applied course will be taught synchronously and involve significant interaction with the course instructor and other students.

courses.title: Regulatory Strategy
courses.description: This advanced pharmaceutical science course will train students to integrate strategic business needs, risk assessment, and risk management when developing a regulatory plan. Using case studies and team projects, students will learn to start with the end in mind, analyze critical product life cycle events, and leverage previous experience to successfully achieve regulatory goals. This graduate-level applied course will be taught synchronously and involve significant interaction with the course instructor other students.

courses.title: Foundations in Implementation Science: Examples in Precision Health and Society
courses.description: The goals of implementation science and precision health are to figure out ways to get the right care to the right patients at the right time. Implementation science is defined as "the study of methods to promote the translation of evidence-based practices, interventions, and policies related to precision health into practice settings to improve patient and population health." This course will cover the fundamentals of implementation science using examples in precision health.

courses.title: Special Topics in Pharmaceutical Sciences
courses.description: Topic determined by instructor and announced in advance.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Seminar in Pharmaceutical Sciences
courses.description: This course is required for all Pharmaceutical Sciences graduate students. Other students must obtain permission from the divisional course director. Class format consists of seminar presentations by students and/or faculty or invited speakers. Students are expected to actively engage in seminar activities and discussions.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Practicum in Pharmaceutical Sciences
courses.description: Enrollment in this variable credit course requires a signed agreement between the Chair of the student's academic division and a representative of the institutional sponsor providing the research practicum. Teaching/learning methods consist of a pharmaceutical sciences-based research training experience at the participating institution involving independent work and written and oral reports.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Research in Pharmaceutical Sciences
courses.description: This is a variable credit course required for all Pharmaceutical Sciences graduate students by their second semester. Teaching/learning methods consist of a pharmaceutical sciences-based mentored research training experience involving independent work and research reports that must be filed at the end of the semester.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Master's (Non-Thesis)
courses.description: Students register for thesis substitute credits after successfully passing their comprehensive written examinations. A minimum of 3 credit hours of thesis substitute research and writing is required for Pharmaceutical Sciences graduate students.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Master's Research and Thesis
courses.description: Students register for thesis credits after successfully passing their comprehensive written examination. A minimum of 3 credit hours of thesis research and writing is required for Pharmaceutical Sciences graduate students.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Doctoral Research and Dissertation
courses.description: Students register for dissertation credits after successfully passing their qualifying preliminary and oral examinations. A minimum of 6 credit hours of dissertation research and writing is required for Pharmaceutical Sciences graduate students.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Adapted Physical Activity
courses.description: Assignments to this class are made for students with special needs in physical education focusing primarily on acute and chronic physical limitations. Activities are assigned commensurate with interests and abilities. Students are required to present an exercise prescription from a physician including prescribed activities and limitations.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 4 total credits. 4 total completions.
courses.gradingStatus: Letter grade; credit hours may not be used toward degree.

courses.title: Beginning Aerobics
courses.description: Provides a cardiovascular fitness program incorporating physiologically safe dance and exercise movements to music. It develops strength, flexibility, and improved cardiorespiratory efficiency.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 4 total credits. 4 total completions.
courses.gradingStatus: Letter grade; credit hours may not be used toward degree.

courses.title: Aerobic Circuit Training
courses.description: Challenges students to achieve higher levels of overall fitness in a cardiovascular program that combines stations of muscular strength with endurance while incorporating a wide variety of equipment. Students are expected to be able to participate in a minimum of 20 minutes of aerobic exercise.
courses.repeatRules: May be repeated for credit. 4 total credits. 4 total completions.
courses.gradingStatus: Letter grade; credit hours may not be used toward degree.

courses.title: Badminton
